name: Classic-Style Test 3
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Swim coach: Sports scientists warn that teenage swimmers who train more than twenty hours a week face a higher risk of shoulder injury. But this warning is overblown. Throughout high school I trained more than twenty-five hours a week, and I never injured a shoulder once.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the swim coach's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: attacks the motives of the sports scientists rather than the evidence for their warning
treats a single person's experience as though it could show that a claim about increased risk is exaggerated
assumes that what is true of swimmers must also be true of athletes in other sports
fails to consider that the coach may have trained fewer hours than the coach now remembers
concludes that heavy training is beneficial merely because it caused no harm in one case
questions.explanation: A warning about higher risk says injuries are more likely, not certain, so one swimmer who escaped injury does nothing to show the risk is overstated; (B) names this anecdote-versus-general-claim flaw. (D) is tempting but merely possible: nothing suggests the coach misremembers, and even accurate memory wouldn't rescue the argument. (E) treats 'not harmful' as 'beneficial,' a conclusion the coach never draws.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The scientists' warning about shoulder injuries in heavy-training teen swimmers is overblown.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The coach trained 25+ hours a week in high school and never hurt a shoulder.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the coach never got hurt? A higher risk means more injuries across many swimmers, not an injury for every single one. This is the anecdote-vs.-general-claim flaw (an 'appeal to anecdote'); it's a classic, know it. It's like saying seatbelt warnings are overblown because your cousin never wore one and never got hurt. We need an answer that says the coach uses one case to dismiss a claim about likelihood.

choices.note: The coach never says anything about the scientists' motives. Wrong flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The scientists who issued this warning are paid by a physical therapy company, so we can ignore what they say.

choices.note: CORRECT. One swimmer's injury-free career is the entire evidence, and a risk claim is about how often injuries happen across many swimmers. A single counterexample can't show the risk is exaggerated.
There's no jump to other sports anywhere in the argument. This is right topic, wrong group.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Heavy training didn't hurt my shoulders as a swimmer, so it won't hurt the shoulders of pitchers or tennis players either.

choices.note: Tempting, because it hints that the coach's story might be unreliable. But it's merely possible: nothing suggests the coach misremembers, and even with perfect memory one swimmer can't refute a claim about risk.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: I'm sure I studied four hours a night in college, so four hours a night is clearly enough to get top grades.

choices.note: The coach says the warning is overblown, not that heavy training is good for you. 'Didn't hurt' isn't 'helped.' This answer adds a conclusion and confuses a polar opposite with a logical one.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Skipping breakfast never made me sick, so skipping breakfast must be good for your health.

questions.stimulus: Many shoppers judge how fresh a bakery's bread is by whether it is still warm. Bakers, however, judge freshness by how recently the dough was mixed. Some bakeries bake loaves throughout the day from dough mixed days earlier and kept frozen, while others bake once before dawn from dough mixed the night before. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: shoppers who buy bread while it is still warm are likely to get the freshest loaves a bakery sells
bread made from frozen dough tastes worse than bread made from dough mixed the night before
most bakeries now bake their bread from dough that has been mixed and frozen days in advance
a loaf that is no longer warm may be fresher than a loaf that has just come out of the oven
shoppers should buy bread only from bakeries that bake once a day from freshly mixed dough
questions.explanation: By the bakers' standard, a dawn loaf from dough mixed the night before can be cool by afternoon yet fresher than a warm loaf baked from days-old frozen dough, so warmth can mislead (D). (A) simply repeats the popular view the passage is pushing back on. (B) shifts from freshness to taste, and (E) adds a recommendation the facts don't support.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Shoppers use warmth as a freshness signal; 2) bakers measure freshness by when the dough was mixed; 3) some bakeries bake all day from days-old frozen dough; 4) others bake once at dawn from dough mixed the night before.

breakdown.analysis: Is warm really the same as fresh? Not by the bakers' measure. Line up the facts: 1. bakers measure freshness by when the dough was mixed; 2. all-day bakeries bake warm loaves from days-old frozen dough; 3. dawn bakeries bake from last night's dough, and those loaves are cool by afternoon. So at 3 p.m. the cool loaf can be the fresher one. We need an answer that says warmth can mislead: a cool loaf may be fresher. The author is pushing back on a popular view, so expect a trap that just repeats it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the familiar view the passage opens with. But the passage is pushing back on it: warm loaves at the all-day bakeries come from days-old dough. Repeating the view the author rejects is a classic completion trap.
The passage never talks about taste. Wrong dimension: freshness (when the dough was mixed) is not flavor.
'Some bakeries' do this; nothing says most. Unsupported quantity.
CORRECT. A cool dawn loaf from last night's dough can be fresher than a warm loaf from days-old frozen dough. 'May be' is exactly as strong as the facts allow.
Adds a 'should' and an 'only' the passage never earns. The argument is about how to judge freshness, not where people must shop.

questions.stimulus: Transit analyst: In January, Corliss City raised the fare on its Route 9 bus, alone among the city's routes, from $2 to $3. Over the following six months, weekend ridership on Route 9 fell by a fifth. The fare increase, therefore, drove weekend riders away from Route 9.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the transit analyst's argument?
choices: Over the same six months, weekend ridership on the city's other bus routes, whose fares did not change, held steady.
Some riders who still take Route 9 on weekends say they would prefer to pay a lower fare.
The fare revenue Route 9 collects on weekends rose slightly despite the drop in ridership.
A bike-share program opened along Route 9's weekend corridor shortly before the fare increase took effect.
Bus fares in Corliss City are higher than those in most cities of comparable size.
questions.explanation: To blame the fare increase, the analyst needs the drop not to have happened anyway; (A) shows that comparable routes without a fare change saw no drop over the same period, ruling out citywide causes like weather or a weekend slump. (D) weakens by offering an alternative cause. (B) is about riders who stayed, not the ones who left.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The fare increase drove weekend riders away from Route 9.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Only Route 9's fare rose; afterward its weekend ridership fell 20%.

breakdown.analysis: Would weekend ridership have dropped anyway, from winter weather or a citywide slump? If so, the fare is off the hook. Blaming a cause means assuming the outcome wouldn't have happened without it. We need an answer that supplies a control group: routes with no fare hike that didn't lose riders.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same city, same months, no fare change, no drop. That rules out the 'it would have happened anyway' explanations and points at the one thing that differed: the fare.
Right topic, wrong group. These are riders who stayed. Everyone prefers lower prices; that doesn't show the price made anyone leave.
Wrong dimension. Revenue isn't the issue; the claim is about why riders left.
Opposite. A new bike-share along the same corridor is an alternative cause, so this weakens.
Comparison to other cities doesn't touch why Route 9's ridership dropped after January. Irrelevant comparison.

questions.stimulus: Since Brightwater Hospital introduced a new discharge checklist, the share of its patients who are readmitted within thirty days has fallen substantially. Yet the hospital's quality board still describes Brightwater's readmission rate as unacceptably high.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Completing the checklist takes nurses about fifteen minutes for each patient who is discharged.
Some patients readmitted since the checklist was introduced were discharged without it being used.
Before the checklist, Brightwater's readmission rate was nearly double the regional average, and it remains well above that average.
Administrators at other hospitals in the region regard Brightwater's checklist as a model worth copying.
Patients discharged using the checklist report greater satisfaction with their care than earlier patients did.
questions.explanation: 'Fallen substantially' is relative to Brightwater's own past, while 'unacceptably high' is an absolute judgment; if the rate started at nearly twice the regional average, a big drop can still leave it too high (C). (B) is merely possible and doesn't show why the board still judges the overall rate high. (A) and (E) are about time and satisfaction, not the rate.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The readmission rate fell a lot after the checklist, but the board still calls it unacceptably high.

breakdown.analysis: Can something fall a lot and still be too high? Of course. A 300-pound person who loses 60 pounds is still heavy. Watch the switch from a relative word (fallen) to an absolute one (high); it's a favorite paradox device. We need an answer that says the rate started so high that even after the drop it remains above an acceptable level.

choices.note: Wrong dimension: nurse time is a cost of the checklist, not a reason the rate is still high.
Merely possible and too vague to help. It suggests the checklist could do more, but it doesn't explain why the overall rate is still judged unacceptable.
CORRECT. The starting point was nearly twice the regional norm. A substantial drop from there can still leave the rate well above average, which is why the board still calls it too high.
Right topic, wrong group. Other hospitals' praise for the checklist says nothing about where Brightwater's rate stands now, and it deepens the puzzle rather than resolving it.
Wrong dimension. Satisfaction is not the readmission rate.

questions.stimulus: Political analyst: In Harlow's council election this fall, turnout fell from 41 percent to 33 percent. It was the first council election since the city stopped mailing a sample ballot to every household. So the city's decision to stop mailing sample ballots reduced turnout.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the political analyst's argument?
choices: Most residents who received sample ballots in earlier elections read them before voting.
Turnout in Harlow's council elections is generally lower than turnout in its mayoral elections.
The money the city saved by not mailing sample ballots was less than the value of the lost turnout.
No resident who received a sample ballot in the previous council election failed to vote in it.
Turnout in this fall's council election would not have fallen just as far had the city continued mailing sample ballots.
questions.explanation: To say the decision reduced turnout, the analyst must assume the drop wouldn't have happened anyway; if turnout would have fallen just as far with sample ballots, the decision caused nothing (E). (A) is tempting but too strong: even if only some residents read the ballots, the decision could still have lowered turnout. (D) is far too strong, and (C) shifts to cost.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Stopping the sample-ballot mailings reduced turnout.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Turnout fell from 41% to 33% in the first election without the mailings.

breakdown.analysis: What if turnout would have dropped just as much anyway? Then the mailings decision caused nothing. Any time an argument blames an action for an outcome, it assumes the outcome wouldn't have happened without that action. Think of a defense lawyer: 'It would have happened anyway.' We need an answer that shuts that defense down. Test by negation.

choices.note: Tempting, because the ballots can only have mattered if people used them. But 'most' is too strong. Negate it: maybe only 30% read them, and losing them could still cost votes. The argument survives.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most residents who received sample ballots read them before voting.

choices.note: Irrelevant comparison. Mayoral races aren't in the argument. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: Turnout in council elections is not generally lower than in mayoral elections.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Whether the decision was worth it financially is a different question from whether it reduced turnout. Negation doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: The money saved was at least as great as the value of the lost turnout.

choices.note: Way too strong: 'no resident' failed to vote. Negate it: a few recipients didn't vote. That doesn't touch the claim that removing ballots lowered turnout.
choices.negation: At least one resident who received a sample ballot in the previous election did not vote.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: turnout would have fallen just as far even with sample ballots mailed. Then the decision made no difference, and the conclusion that it reduced turnout collapses.
choices.negation: Turnout this fall would have fallen just as far even if the city had kept mailing sample ballots.

questions.stimulus: At Fennick Software, no code change is merged into the main codebase unless at least one engineer other than its author has reviewed it. In addition, every change that affects the payment system must be approved by a security lead before it is merged. Last week, a change that Imani wrote for the search page was merged.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Imani's change to the search page was approved by a security lead before it was merged.
Every change that is reviewed by an engineer other than its author is merged into the main codebase.
If a merged change was not approved by a security lead, then that change does not affect the payment system.
Imani's change to the search page did not affect the payment system in any way.
Changes that affect the payment system are reviewed more carefully than other changes are.
questions.explanation: The second rule says payment-system change AND merged → security-lead approval; its contrapositive is that a merged change without that approval doesn't affect the payment system, which is (C). (D) is tempting, but nothing says a search-page change can't touch the payment system, so it isn't guaranteed. (B) reverses the first rule: review is required for merging, not enough for it.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Merged → reviewed by someone other than the author; 2) affects payment system AND merged → approved by a security lead; 3) Imani's search-page change was merged.

breakdown.analysis: What do we actually know about Imani's change? Only that it was merged. Write the rules as arrows: 1. merged → reviewed by another engineer; 2. payment-system change AND merged → security-lead approval. Contrapositive of 2: merged AND no security approval → not a payment-system change. Hard to prephrase a specific answer; watch for reversed arrows and for claims about Imani that the rules don't force.

choices.note: Only payment-system changes need security approval, and we don't know Imani's did. Could be true, need not be.
Reverses rule 1. Review is necessary for merging, not sufficient. A reviewed change could still be rejected.
CORRECT. This is the contrapositive of rule 2. The awkward 'if not approved... then does not affect' wording is how the LSAT hides a right answer.
Tempting, because 'search page' sounds unrelated to payments. But we don't know this: nothing says a search-page change can't touch the payment system. It could be true, but it isn't forced.
Unsupported comparison. The rules require an extra approval, but nothing says anyone reviews more carefully. 'More carefully' stretches the facts.

questions.stimulus: Wildlife biologist: We fitted forty red squirrels in Alder Wood with tracking collars. Throughout the autumn, the squirrels spent about 70 percent of their foraging time within twenty meters of a hazel tree. Clearly, the red squirrels of Alder Wood prefer to forage near hazel trees.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the wildlife biologist's argument?
choices: About 75 percent of the area of Alder Wood lies within twenty meters of a hazel tree.
Red squirrels in most other woodlands spend the bulk of their foraging time near oak trees.
Hazelnuts are among the most nutritious foods available to red squirrels in autumn.
Some of the collared squirrels spent even more of their time near hazel trees in spring than in autumn.
Tracking collars can slightly reduce the distance that a squirrel travels in a single day.
questions.explanation: A preference means squirrels forage near hazels more than chance would predict, so the argument needs a baseline: how much of the wood is near a hazel. If 75 percent of the wood is, then spending 70 percent of the time there shows no preference at all (A). (C) strengthens, and (E) is merely possible and doesn't say which way any bias would run.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Alder Wood's red squirrels prefer foraging near hazel trees.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Collared squirrels spent ~70% of autumn foraging time within 20 m of a hazel.

breakdown.analysis: 70 percent compared to what? If almost the whole wood is near a hazel, squirrels wandering at random would rack up 70 percent anyway. This is a missing-comparison-group problem: the data describe one group with no baseline. It's like saying a student 'prefers' libraries because she spends 70% of her day on a campus that's 75% libraries. We need an answer showing that hazel-adjacent ground is about as common as the squirrels' time there.

choices.note: CORRECT. If 75% of the wood is within 20 m of a hazel, squirrels spending 70% of their time there are doing slightly less than chance. No preference shown.
Wrong group. The conclusion is only about Alder Wood's squirrels. What squirrels elsewhere do doesn't touch it.
Opposite. A good reason to seek out hazels makes the preference more believable, so this strengthens.
Different season and only 'some' squirrels. It doesn't undercut the autumn data; if anything it's mildly consistent with a hazel preference.
Merely possible bias with no direction. Shorter travel doesn't say the squirrels would end up near hazels more or less often. You can't weaken on a 'maybe.'

questions.stimulus:
Rosa: The Halvard Museum should start charging admission. A modest fee would pay for longer opening hours, and at other museums that introduced such fees, attendance barely changed.

Tomas: Overall attendance might well hold steady. But free admission is what brings families from the low-income neighborhoods around the museum, and even a modest fee would keep many of them away. The museum should stay free.
questions.stem: Rosa and Tomas disagree over whether
choices: a modest admission fee would generate enough money to pay for longer opening hours
overall attendance at the Halvard Museum would drop sharply if an admission fee were introduced
families from low-income neighborhoods value the museum more than other visitors do
the Halvard Museum should begin charging an admission fee
the museum's duty to nearby neighborhoods outweighs every other consideration
questions.explanation: Rosa says the museum should charge admission and Tomas says it should stay free, so they disagree on (D). (B) is the trap: Tomas concedes overall attendance might hold steady, so he doesn't disagree with Rosa there. Neither speaker addresses (C) or the sweeping claim in (E), and Tomas never disputes (A).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Rosa: charge a fee; it funds longer hours and doesn't hurt attendance. Tomas: overall attendance may hold, but a fee would drive away low-income families; stay free.

breakdown.analysis: Where does one say yes and the other say no? To disagree, one speaker must take a side the other rejects. Their last lines are direct opposites: 'should start charging' vs. 'should stay free.' Notice Tomas's concession ('attendance might well hold steady'); that's where the trap lives.

choices.note: Rosa says yes; Tomas never addresses funding. No disagreement on record.

Tempting, because attendance is a big part of Rosa's case. But Tomas concedes overall attendance might well hold steady. If anything they agree here, and to disagree one must say yes and the other no.
Unsupported comparison. Tomas says a fee would keep these families away, not that they value the museum more than others do.
CORRECT. Rosa: should charge. Tomas: should stay free. Yes vs. no on the same question.
Too strong. Tomas weighs one consideration heavily, but 'outweighs every other consideration' goes far beyond him, and Rosa never discusses it.

questions.stimulus: Curator Lund defines a forgery as any artwork created with the intention that it be mistaken for the work of a different artist. But imagine a painter who, to train her hand, makes an exact copy of a famous canvas and keeps it in her studio, telling no one. If her nephew later sells the copy as the original, the copy is surely a forgery, though it was never created to deceive anyone. So Lund's definition is inadequate.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that because Lund's definition is widely accepted among curators, it is likely to be correct
showing that Lund's definition contradicts another claim that Lund has made about forgeries
questioning Lund's expertise in determining whether an artwork is authentic
describing a case that meets Lund's definition but that the author holds is not a forgery
describing a case that Lund's definition excludes but that the author holds is a forgery
questions.explanation: The copy was not created to deceive, so Lund's definition doesn't count it as a forgery, yet the author says it is one; the definition is shown to be too narrow (E). (D) is the mirror-image trap, the 'too broad' objection: it would require a case the definition includes that shouldn't be included. (A) runs opposite to the argument, which rejects the definition.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Lund's definition of forgery is inadequate.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A private practice copy later sold as an original is a forgery, but it wasn't created to deceive, so Lund's definition leaves it out.

breakdown.analysis: Does the painter's copy fit Lund's definition? No: it wasn't created to deceive. Yet the author calls it a forgery anyway. So the definition leaves out something it should include: it's too narrow. It's like defining 'chair' as 'a seat with four legs' and pointing at a three-legged chair. We need an answer that says: a case outside the definition that should be inside. Expect a mirror-image 'too broad' trap.

choices.note: The author rejects the definition; there's no appeal to popularity here. Opposite of the argument's direction.
choices.example: Example of this method: Most curators accept Lund's definition, so it is probably right.

choices.note: The argument never cites any other claim of Lund's. It uses a hypothetical case, not an internal contradiction.
choices.example: Example of this method: Lund says a forgery requires intent to deceive, yet Lund also calls an innocent copy a forgery, so Lund contradicts herself.

choices.note: No attack on Lund's credentials. This describes an ad hominem the argument doesn't make.
choices.example: Example of this method: Lund has never authenticated a painting, so her definition of forgery can't be trusted.

choices.note: Tempting, because it describes the same method in mirror image (the 'too broad' objection). But the copy does not meet Lund's definition, since there was no intent to deceive, so the case falls outside the definition, not inside.
choices.example: Example of this method: By Lund's definition, an actor's prop painting made to look like a Rembrandt for a film is a forgery, but surely it isn't.

choices.note: CORRECT. The copy fails Lund's intent test, so her definition excludes it, but the author says it's surely a forgery. Definition too narrow.

questions.stimulus: Hospital policy analyst: A hospital should postpone a scheduled nonemergency surgery whenever no fully rested anesthesiologist is available for it or the equipment it requires has not passed its most recent safety check, provided that the delay would not put the patient at serious risk.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated by the hospital policy analyst?
choices: Ward Hospital was right to postpone Mr. Ansel's scheduled gallbladder surgery because its only available anesthesiologist had just worked a double shift, even though his surgeon warned that a delay would put him at serious risk.

Carver Hospital was right to postpone Ms. Ito's scheduled knee replacement because the surgical drill it required had failed its latest safety check, even though a fully rested anesthesiologist was available and a week's delay posed no serious risk.
Linton Hospital was right to proceed with Ms. Reyes's scheduled hernia repair using an exhausted anesthesiologist, because a delay would have inconvenienced her family.

Pine Hospital was right to postpone Mr. Dorr's scheduled cataract surgery because the surgeon was tired, although a fully rested anesthesiologist was available, the equipment had passed inspection, and a delay posed no risk.
Mercy Hospital was right to proceed with Mr. Lau's emergency appendectomy using a tired anesthesiologist, because any delay would have endangered his life.
questions.explanation: The principle says: nonemergency surgery AND (no rested anesthesiologist OR equipment not passed) AND delay not seriously risky → postpone. (B) meets it through the equipment half of the 'or' and satisfies the risk proviso. (A) has a trigger but fails the proviso, and (D) is the tempting trap: a tired surgeon is neither trigger.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Nonemergency surgery AND (no fully rested anesthesiologist OR equipment hasn't passed its latest safety check) AND delay not seriously risky → postpone.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The right answer must show a hospital postponing a nonemergency surgery where 1. at least one of the two triggers is present and 2. the delay posed no serious risk.

breakdown.analysis: Does a tired anyone count, or only a tired anesthesiologist? Only the anesthesiologist, and the other trigger is failed equipment. The 'or' means either trigger is enough, but the risk proviso is required either way. We need an answer that checks: nonemergency, one trigger, safe delay, and the action 'postpone.' Each trap satisfies only part.

choices.note: A trigger is present (exhausted anesthesiologist), but the separate condition fails: the delay was seriously risky. The principle doesn't back postponing here.
CORRECT. Nonemergency, the drill failed its check (second half of the 'or'), the delay was safe, and the hospital postponed. A rested anesthesiologist doesn't matter, because one trigger is enough.
This reverses what the principle says. A trigger is present and family inconvenience isn't serious risk to the patient, so the principle says postpone, not proceed.

Tempting. Fatigue, a safe delay, and postponement all sound right. But the principle's triggers are an unrested anesthesiologist or failed equipment, and here neither is present. A tired surgeon is outside the rule.
Outside the scope: the principle covers only nonemergency surgery. Proceeding may be right, but we don't know that from this principle.

questions.stimulus: In an anonymous survey of all 300 engineers at Quarry Labs, most of the engineers said they believe that the code they write contains fewer bugs than the code written by most of their colleagues at the company.
questions.stem: If the survey responses accurately reflect the engineers' beliefs, which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: At least some engineers at Quarry Labs are mistaken about how their code compares with that of their colleagues.
Most engineers at Quarry Labs are mistaken about how their code compares with that of their colleagues.
The engineers at Quarry Labs who write the fewest bugs are the ones least likely to rate their own code highly.
Engineers at Quarry Labs overrate their own code more than engineers at other companies do.
Most engineers at Quarry Labs write code containing fewer bugs than the company's average.
questions.explanation: Rank the 300 engineers by bug count: at most half of them can each have fewer bugs than most of their colleagues, so if more than half believe they do, at least one belief is wrong (A). (B) is the trap: the facts allow as few as one mistaken engineer. (C) echoes a familiar story about self-assessment that the survey says nothing about.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) All 300 engineers surveyed; 2) most (151+) believe their code has fewer bugs than most (more than half) of their colleagues'; 3) responses reflect real beliefs.

breakdown.analysis: Can most people really beat most of their colleagues? Line everyone up from fewest bugs to most: only the top half can each beat more than half of the others. So at most 150 engineers can be right, and more than 150 believe it. At least one is wrong, and that's all you get. 'Most believe' doesn't mean 'most are wrong': the mistaken ones could be just a handful. Worked example: if exactly 151 believe it and the 150 best coders are among them, only one person is mistaken.

choices.note: CORRECT. At most half can actually beat most of their colleagues, and more than half believe they do. So at least one belief is false.
Tempting, because so many engineers seem overconfident. But it's too strong: the math only guarantees one mistaken engineer. If the 151 believers include the 150 best coders, just one is wrong.
Social autopilot: it echoes a familiar story about overconfident weak performers. The survey gives no information about which engineers hold which beliefs.
Wrong group. No other company appears in the facts.
Merely possible. With a few very buggy coders dragging the average up, most could be below average, but nothing says that's so here. 'Average' is a different measure from 'most colleagues.'

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Supporters of ranked-choice voting claim it reduces negative campaigning. Their evidence is a single city where attack ads declined after the system was adopted. But attack ads declined nationwide that same year, so that city's experience proves nothing. Ranked-choice voting, therefore, does not reduce negative campaigning.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: attacks the motives of the supporters of ranked-choice voting rather than the evidence they offer
relies on nationwide figures that may not reflect conditions in the city the supporters cite
treats the failure of the supporters' evidence to establish their claim as showing that the claim is false
presumes without justification that negative campaigning is harmful to voters
concludes that ranked-choice voting is undesirable because it fails to achieve one of its intended goals
questions.explanation: The columnist shows that the supporters' evidence is weak, which at most leaves their claim unproven; concluding that ranked-choice voting does not reduce negative campaigning treats a failed argument as a disproof (C). (B) is merely possible and would, if anything, quibble with the columnist's rebuttal rather than identify the leap to the conclusion. (E) adds a conclusion about desirability that the columnist never draws.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ranked-choice voting does not reduce negative campaigning.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The supporters' only evidence (one city's drop in attack ads) is undercut by a nationwide drop that same year.

breakdown.analysis: Does knocking down the supporters' evidence prove they're wrong? No. It leaves their claim unproven. The rebuttal itself is fine (a national trend undercuts one city's data). The flaw is treating a failed argument as proof the conclusion is false; it's a classic, know it. It's like saying: your only witness was unreliable, so the defendant is innocent. We need an answer that names the jump from 'not shown' to 'false.'

choices.note: No motives are discussed. The columnist addresses the evidence directly.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Supporters of ranked-choice voting are mostly third-party activists who'd benefit from it, so their claims can be dismissed.

choices.note: Tempting, because it pokes at the columnist's national figures. But it's merely possible, and it aims at the wrong step. Even if the national figures fit the city perfectly, the jump from 'unproven' to 'false' would still be the flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Attendance rose nationwide this year, so it must have risen at our local theater too.

choices.note: CORRECT. Showing the evidence proves nothing is not the same as proving the opposite. The conclusion 'does not reduce' needs its own evidence.
The columnist never says anything about whether negative campaigning harms voters. Adds an assumption the argument doesn't need.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Negative ads are common in close races, so they must be hurting voters.

choices.note: Adds a conclusion the columnist never draws. The columnist talks only about whether the system reduces attack ads, not whether it's undesirable.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new bus lane didn't cut commute times, so the city should tear it out.

questions.stimulus: Hospital researcher: Of the patients at Linden General who developed infections after surgery last year, 60 percent had received a pre-operative antiseptic wash made with the hospital's new formula. Clearly, the new formula does little to prevent post-surgical infections.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the hospital researcher's argument?
choices: How much more does the new antiseptic formula cost the hospital than the formula it replaced?
Did any of the patients who received the new formula report skin irritation after the wash?
What percentage of post-surgical infections at other hospitals are successfully treated with antibiotics?
What percentage of all surgical patients at Linden General last year received a wash made with the new formula?
Were most of the patients who developed infections given antibiotics after their surgeries?
questions.explanation: The 60 percent figure means nothing without knowing how common the new wash was among all surgical patients: if 95 percent received it, the washed patients were underrepresented among infections and the formula looks effective; if 60 percent did, it looks useless (D). (E) is tempting, but it describes only the infected group again and gives no comparison between washed and unwashed patients.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new antiseptic formula does little to prevent post-surgical infections.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 60% of patients who got infections had used the new wash.

breakdown.analysis: Sixty percent of infections had the wash. Out of how many patients who had the wash? Without knowing how common the wash was among all patients, the 60 percent is meaningless. Missing comparison group again. It's like saying most car crashes involve sober drivers, so sobriety doesn't help. Most drivers are sober! We need the question that supplies the baseline.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Cost has nothing to do with whether the wash prevents infection.
Wrong dimension. Side effects aren't effectiveness.
Wrong group and wrong question: other hospitals, and treatment after infection rather than prevention.

CORRECT. This is the baseline. Compare the share of infected patients who had the wash (60%) with the share of all patients who had it, and you can tell whether the wash lowers, raises, or doesn't change the infection rate.

Tempting, because antibiotics sound like a hidden factor. But it asks only about the infected patients again. Without a comparison to uninfected patients, any answer leaves the argument just as hard to judge.

questions.stimulus: Bakery owner: We will add the cardamom bun to our permanent menu only if it can be made entirely from ingredients sold by our current suppliers. Cardamom of the quality the bun's recipe calls for is sold only by specialty importers, and none of our current suppliers is a specialty importer. So the cardamom bun will not be added to our permanent menu.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the bakery owner's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If the cardamom bun could be made entirely from ingredients sold by current suppliers, it would be added to the permanent menu.
Specialty importers charge more for cardamom than the bakery's current suppliers charge for any other spice.
Some of the bakery's current suppliers could begin importing high-quality cardamom within the year.
If the bakery had cardamom of the quality the recipe calls for, it would be able to make the cardamom bun.
The cardamom bun cannot be made without cardamom of the quality its recipe calls for.
questions.explanation: The premises show the current suppliers don't sell recipe-quality cardamom, but the conclusion needs that cardamom to be necessary for the bun; (E) supplies that necessary condition, so the bun can't be made entirely from current suppliers' ingredients and won't be added. (D) is the trap: it gives the sufficient version (having the cardamom lets the bun be made), which leaves open that the bun could be made with other cardamom. (A) reverses the owner's 'only if' rule.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The cardamom bun won't be added to the permanent menu.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Permanent menu → can be made entirely from current suppliers' ingredients; recipe-quality cardamom → sold only by specialty importers; no current supplier is a specialty importer.

breakdown.analysis: Who says the bun needs the fancy cardamom? Maybe cheaper cardamom works fine. Chain what we have: 1. permanent menu → makeable entirely from current suppliers; 2. recipe-quality cardamom → sold only by importers; 3. current suppliers aren't importers. So current suppliers lack recipe-quality cardamom. Missing link: bun → requires recipe-quality cardamom. Full chain: bun needs that cardamom → current suppliers lack it → bun not makeable from current suppliers → (contrapositive of 1) not on the permanent menu. We need the necessary-condition version of the link, and a trap will offer the sufficient version.

choices.note: Reverses the conditional. The owner said makeable is necessary, and this treats it as sufficient. It also tells us nothing about whether the bun is makeable, so the conclusion still doesn't follow.
Wrong dimension. Price isn't in the rule; the rule is about who sells the ingredients.
Merely possible, and it pushes toward the bun being added later. That's the opposite of what we need.

Tempting. It connects cardamom and the bun, but in the wrong direction: it makes recipe-quality cardamom sufficient for the bun. We need it to be necessary (no such cardamom → no bun). Knowing what having it would allow tells us nothing about whether the bun can be made without it.

CORRECT. Now the bun requires recipe-quality cardamom, which no current supplier sells, so the bun can't be made entirely from current suppliers' ingredients. The rule's necessary condition fails, and the bun stays off the menu.

questions.stimulus: Transit official: After bus-only lanes opened on Grant Avenue in March, the average time a bus needed to travel the length of the avenue fell by six minutes. Yet in the months since, a larger share of Grant Avenue buses have arrived late at their stops than did before the lanes opened.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain how Grant Avenue buses could be arriving late more often even though their travel times have fallen?
choices: Ridership on Grant Avenue buses increased after the lanes opened, as riders were attracted by faster trips.
When the lanes opened, the transit agency revised the Grant Avenue timetable, cutting the scheduled travel time on the avenue by ten minutes.
Buses on several routes that do not use Grant Avenue have also arrived late more often since March.
Delivery trucks occasionally park illegally in the bus lanes, blocking buses for several minutes at a time.
Drivers of private cars on Grant Avenue complain that the bus lanes have made their own trips slower.
questions.explanation: 'Late' is measured against the timetable, not against the old travel time; if the schedule was cut by ten minutes while actual trips got only six minutes faster, buses are quicker than before yet more often behind schedule (B). (D) is tempting, but occasional blockages are already reflected in the six-minute average improvement and don't explain why lateness increased. (C) concerns other routes.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Buses got six minutes faster on Grant Avenue, but they're late more often than before.

breakdown.analysis: Faster than what, and late compared to what? 'Faster' is measured against the old trips; 'late' is measured against the timetable. If the timetable changed, both can be true. Think of a runner who improves her mile by 6 seconds while her coach tightens the target by 10: she's faster and misses her target more often. We need an answer that says the schedule got tighter than the real improvement.

choices.note: Tempting, because more riders means longer boarding times. But the six-minute improvement already reflects real trips with those riders, so this doesn't explain more lateness against the schedule.
CORRECT. Schedule cut by 10 minutes, actual trips cut by 6. Buses are faster but now 4 minutes behind the old cushion, so more of them run late.
Wrong group. Other routes' lateness doesn't explain how Grant Avenue buses got faster and later at once.
Tempting, because blocked lanes obviously delay buses. But those blockages were part of the trips that still averaged six minutes faster; occasional delays don't explain why lateness rose.
Wrong group: car drivers. Their slower trips say nothing about bus lateness.

questions.stimulus: Last season, none of the players in the Ridgeback youth soccer club who attended the club's preseason conditioning camp suffered a hamstring injury. This year, every player on the club's roster attended the camp. So no player in the club will suffer a hamstring injury this season.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Last year, no painting at the Pell Museum that was fitted with a humidity monitor developed mold. This year, every painting in the museum has been fitted with one. So no painting at the Pell Museum will develop mold this year.

Last year, every Elm Line bus that received new brakes passed its safety inspection. This year, some Elm Line buses did not receive new brakes. So some Elm Line buses will fail their safety inspection this year.
Last year, every employee at Fairfax Bakery who completed the food-safety course passed the health inspection. So completing the course is what enabled those employees to pass.

Last year, no volunteer at the Bayside clinic who attended orientation quit before the year ended. This year, no volunteer at the clinic has quit. So every volunteer this year must have attended orientation.
Last season, the Comets' players who lifted weights had fewer injuries than those who only stretched. So lifting weights is the most effective way for any athlete to avoid injury.
questions.explanation: The argument takes a past pattern (no one who did X had problem Y), notes that now everyone in the group has done X, and predicts no one will have Y; (A) matches step for step. (B) reasons from those who lacked X to a predicted problem, (D) reverses the direction, and (C) and (E) draw causal or superlative conclusions without any 'now everyone has X' step.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: No club player will suffer a hamstring injury this season.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last season, no camp attendee was hurt; this year every player attended.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Last time, no one who did X had Y; now everyone in the group has done X; so no one in the group will have Y.

breakdown.analysis: Does last year's luck guarantee this year's? No, and that's why the argument is shaky. But the question asks only for the same pattern. Map it: 1. last time, no one who did X had Y; 2. now everyone in the group has done X; 3. so no one in the group will have Y. We need a choice with all three pieces in the same roles.

choices.note: CORRECT. Past: no monitored painting got mold. Now: every painting is monitored. Prediction: no mold. Same three steps.
Different shape: it reasons from the ones who didn't get X to a prediction that some will fail. That's a negated version, not the same pattern.
No 'now everyone has X' step and no prediction; it draws a causal conclusion about last year instead.

Tempting, because it uses the same past-pattern setup and topic flavor. But this reverses the direction: it goes from the outcome (no one quit) back to the condition (all attended). The original goes from condition to predicted outcome.
Unsupported superlative ('most effective') and a comparison between two groups. Different pattern entirely.

questions.stimulus: It is widely believed that feeding birds in winter makes them dependent on feeders and less able to find natural food. But in a three-year study of black-capped chickadees, birds with access to feeders still got most of their winter food from natural sources, and when the feeders were removed, those birds survived the rest of the winter at the same rate as birds that had never used feeders. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: chickadees that use feeders in winter gradually lose much of their ability to forage on their own
winter feeding improves chickadees' chances of surviving cold winters
at least for chickadees, winter feeding does not appear to create the dependence that many people fear
people need not be concerned about any effects that feeding might have on wild birds
chickadees prefer natural foods to the seeds that are offered at feeders
questions.explanation: The study cuts against the popular dependence worry, but only for chickadees, so (C) is properly limited. (A) restates the popular view the author is rejecting. (B) treats 'no worse off' as 'better off,' and (D) stretches one species and one worry into 'any effects' on 'wild birds.'

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Popular belief: winter feeding makes birds dependent; 2) chickadees with feeders still got most food naturally; 3) after feeders were removed, they survived as well as never-fed birds.

breakdown.analysis: Did the study find dependence? No: the fed birds got most of their food naturally and survived just as well without feeders. The author sets up a popular view and pushes back on it. We need a completion that says the dependence worry isn't borne out, staying as narrow as the evidence (one species, one worry). Expect traps that repeat the popular view or overshoot to 'feeding helps.'

choices.note: This is the popular view the passage is rejecting. The study shows the opposite for chickadees.
Tempting, because the fed birds did fine. But 'no worse off' isn't 'better off.' They survived at the same rate, so this confuses a polar opposite with a logical one.
CORRECT. Matches the evidence and its limits: chickadees, and the dependence worry specifically.
Too broad. One species and one concern can't clear 'any effects' on all wild birds.
Merely possible. Getting most food naturally could reflect availability, not preference.

questions.stimulus: Engineering manager: At the start of last quarter, our team began requiring that every code change be accompanied by automated tests. Last quarter, the number of bugs reported by our customers fell by 30 percent from the previous quarter. So the testing requirement is reducing the number of bugs our customers encounter.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the engineering manager's argument?
choices: Most engineers on the team say that writing the required tests has slowed down their work considerably.
Customer-reported bugs fell by a similar percentage last quarter at several software companies that have no testing requirement.
Automated tests can catch some kinds of bugs that manual code reviews tend to miss.
The drop in customer-reported bugs came almost entirely from parts of the software that were modified after the testing requirement took effect.
Several customers who had reported many bugs in the previous quarter stopped using the team's software before last quarter began.
questions.explanation: If the decline is concentrated in code written under the new requirement, while older untouched code shows no comparable drop, the improvement tracks the requirement rather than a general cause such as fewer customers or an industry-wide trend (D). (C) is the tempting trap: it says only that tests 'can' catch 'some' bugs, which makes the mechanism possible without showing it worked here. (B) and (E) supply alternative explanations and so weaken.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The testing requirement is reducing the bugs customers encounter.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the requirement began, customer-reported bugs fell 30%.

breakdown.analysis: Did the tests cut the bugs, or did something else, like fewer customers or an industry-wide lull? That's correlation vs. causation in a before/after study, the most common flaw on the test. A strong strengthener ties the drop specifically to the code the requirement touched. It's like crediting a new fertilizer: convincing if only the fertilized rows improved. We need an answer that pins the improvement to the tested code.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Speed of work isn't the issue; bug reduction is.
Opposite. A similar drop at companies without the requirement suggests something industry-wide, which weakens.
Tempting, because it supplies a mechanism. But 'can catch some kinds' is so vague it's nearly always true. It shows tests could help in principle, not that they caused this drop.
CORRECT. The decline is concentrated where the requirement applied. A general cause like fewer customers would show up across old and new code alike, so this localizes the effect to the tested code.
Opposite. Losing heavy bug-reporters before the quarter offers an alternative explanation for fewer reports.

questions.stimulus: Track coach: Over the past season, runners on our team who attended the optional film sessions cut their race times by more, on average, than runners who skipped them. So, to improve our team's race times next season, I will require every runner to attend the film sessions.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the track coach's argument requires which one of the following assumptions?
choices: The film sessions are the most valuable part of the team's training program.
At least some of the runners who have been skipping the film sessions would improve more if they attended them.
Every runner who attended the film sessions cut his or her race times by more than every runner who skipped them.
Requiring attendance will not make the film sessions less enjoyable for the runners who already attend them.
The film sessions take up less of the runners' time than their weight-training sessions do.
questions.explanation: Runners who already attend will keep attending, so the plan can improve the team only through those who now skip; if none of them would improve more by attending, requiring attendance gains nothing (B). (D) is tempting but shifts from race times to enjoyment, and its negation doesn't defeat the plan. (A) and (C) are far stronger than the argument needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Requiring film sessions will improve the team's race times.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Runners who chose to attend improved more on average than those who skipped.

breakdown.analysis: Were the film-session runners improving because of film, or because the motivated runners are the ones who show up? Self-selection. And the plan only changes anything for the current skippers, because the attenders already attend. We need: at least some skippers would benefit. Negate it (no skipper would improve) and the plan does nothing.

choices.note: Unsupported superlative. Negate it: film isn't the most valuable part. It can still help, so the argument survives.
choices.negation: The film sessions are not the most valuable part of the team's training program.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: no current skipper would improve more by attending. Then requiring attendance changes nothing that matters, and the plan fails.
choices.negation: None of the runners who have been skipping the film sessions would improve more if they attended them.

choices.note: Way too strong. Negate it: there's some overlap between the groups. The averages can still favor film sessions, and the argument is fine.
choices.negation: At least one runner who attended did not cut his or her time by more than at least one runner who skipped.

choices.note: Tempting, because a resentful team might train worse. But enjoyment isn't race times. Negate it: the sessions get a bit less fun. The coach's goal can still be met, so it isn't required.
choices.negation: Requiring attendance will make the film sessions less enjoyable for the runners who already attend.

choices.note: Irrelevant comparison. Negate it: film takes more time than weights. That says nothing about whether it improves race times.
choices.negation: The film sessions take up at least as much of the runners' time as their weight-training sessions do.

questions.stimulus: Architecture critic: The new wing of the Ostrava Museum is a failure of design. The building simply does not work as architecture, since it falls short in nearly every respect that matters to good design. Admittedly, attendance has climbed since the wing opened. But crowds come for exhibitions, not for buildings, so the rise in attendance says nothing about the wing's merit.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the architecture critic's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that a building that attracts large crowds cannot be well designed
relies on the authority of architecture critics rather than on evidence about the building itself
concludes that the wing fails in every respect when the evidence concerns only its design
fails to consider that attendance may have risen for reasons unrelated to the new wing
offers in support of its conclusion a claim that does little more than restate that conclusion
questions.explanation: The only support offered for 'the wing is a failure of design' is that it 'does not work as architecture' because it 'falls short in nearly every respect that matters to good design,' which is the conclusion in different words (E). (D) is tempting but backward: the critic explicitly considers another reason for the attendance rise. (A) overreads the critic, who says crowds are irrelevant to merit, not that popularity signals bad design.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new wing is a failure of design.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: It doesn't work as architecture because it falls short in nearly every respect that matters to good design; rising attendance is irrelevant because crowds come for exhibitions.

breakdown.analysis: What actual evidence is given that the wing is badly designed? Strip the premise down: 'it falls short in nearly every respect that matters to good design.' That's just 'it's badly designed' again. This is circular reasoning (begging the question); it's a classic, know it. It's like saying 'this movie is boring because it fails to hold your interest.' You might think the flaw is in the attendance part, but that objection is handled reasonably, which is exactly what makes the circular core easy to miss.

choices.note: Polar vs. logical opposite. The critic says crowds say nothing about merit, not that crowds mean bad design.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new wing is packed every weekend, so it must be badly designed; good buildings never attract crowds.

choices.note: No authority is cited. The critic is the speaker, not the evidence.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most architecture critics dislike the new wing, so it must be poorly designed.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about design ('a failure of design'), so there's no overreach to 'every respect.'
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The wing's lighting is poor, so the wing fails as a building, as a gallery, and as an investment.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'overlooks an alternative cause' is so often the right flaw. But here it's backward: the critic does consider another reason for the attendance rise (crowds come for exhibitions).
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Attendance rose after the wing opened, so the wing must have drawn the new visitors.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Falls short in nearly every respect that matters to good design' just restates 'failure of design.' The premise assumes the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Bakery owner: A customer asked us to bake a cake bearing a message that mocked a local charity. We declined. Some say a business should fill any lawful order, but our refusal was justified. The cake was to be displayed at a public event in a box bearing our bakery's name, and people there would reasonably have taken the message to reflect our own views.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the bakery owner's reasoning?
choices: A business should fill every lawful order unless filling it would cause the business to lose money.
A business that declines an order should explain its reasons for doing so to the customer.
A business should not be held responsible for the views expressed in items it makes at a customer's request.
A business may decline a lawful order if the finished item would publicly bear the business's name and would reasonably be taken to express its views.
A message that most people would find offensive should not be displayed at a public event.
questions.explanation: The owner's grounds are that the cake would be publicly tied to the bakery and reasonably read as the bakery's own view; (D) turns exactly those facts into permission to decline. (E) is tempting, but it governs what may be displayed at events, not what a bakery may refuse to make, and nothing says most people would find the message offensive. (C) cuts against the owner by denying that the bakery bears responsibility for the message.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bakery was justified in refusing the cake order.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. The cake would be shown at a public event; 2. the box would carry the bakery's name; 3. people would reasonably read the message as the bakery's view.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the message is nasty? The owner never rests on that. The owner's reason is that the public would reasonably see the message as the bakery's own speech. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, using the facts the argument gives. We need: publicly linked + reasonably read as the business's view → the business may decline.

choices.note: Wrong dimension, and it points the wrong way. Money never comes up, and this rule would require filling the order.
So? Explaining a refusal is a different duty. It doesn't say whether refusing was justified.
Opposite. If the bakery isn't responsible for the message, the owner's main reason for refusing disappears.
CORRECT. Every trigger matches the owner's facts (lawful item, publicly linked to the bakery, reasonably read as its views), and the rule's outcome is permission to decline.

Tempting. It sounds like it backs the refusal. But it's a rule about what events should display, not about what a bakery may refuse to bake, and we don't know that most people would find this message offensive.

questions.stimulus: Biologist: Gray foxes in the Kessel Valley never establish a den in an area where they have detected the scent of coyotes. Yet our recent survey found active gray fox dens in several areas of the valley that coyotes regularly patrol.
questions.stem: If the biologist's statements are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: In some areas that coyotes regularly patrol, gray foxes established dens without having detected the scent of coyotes there.
Coyotes do not leave a detectable scent in every area of the Kessel Valley that they regularly patrol.
Gray foxes are less able to detect the scent of coyotes than are other animals in the Kessel Valley.
Gray foxes that den in areas coyotes patrol are more likely to be killed by coyotes than other gray foxes are.
Most gray fox dens in the Kessel Valley are located in areas that coyotes do not regularly patrol.
questions.explanation: Foxes never den where they've detected coyote scent, yet dens exist in coyote-patrolled areas, so in those areas the foxes established dens without having detected coyote scent (A). (B) is the attractive trap: the foxes might simply have missed scent that was there, or the coyotes may have begun patrolling only after the dens were built, so it need not be true.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Detected coyote scent in an area → no fox den established there; 2. there are active fox dens in several areas coyotes regularly patrol.

breakdown.analysis: So how did the foxes end up denning right on coyote turf? Run the contrapositive: den established in an area → the fox hadn't detected coyote scent there. Combine with fact 2: some coyote-patrolled areas hold dens set up by foxes that hadn't detected coyote scent. That's an existence inference: there are places with coyotes where the foxes didn't know it. Hard to say why they didn't know. Watch for answers that pick one explanation.

choices.note: CORRECT. Contrapositive of fact 1 plus fact 2: in those patrolled areas, the dens were set up by foxes that hadn't detected coyote scent. It doesn't say why, which is why it's guaranteed.

Tempting. It's the most natural explanation. But the foxes could have missed scent that was there, or the coyotes may have started patrolling after the dens were built. One possible explanation isn't a must-be-true.
Wrong group comparison. No other animals are mentioned.
Adds a consequence the facts never mention. We know nothing about fox deaths.
We don't know this. 'Several' dens are in patrolled areas; nothing tells us how many dens there are in total.

questions.stimulus: Campaign strategist: In last year's city council races, the 20 candidates whose campaigns knocked on the doors of more than 5,000 households won 15 seats, while the 30 candidates whose campaigns reached fewer households won only 6. So door-to-door canvassing substantially improves a candidate's chances of winning.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the campaign strategist's argument?
choices: Several of the candidates whose campaigns visited more than 5,000 households lost their races by wide margins.
Door-to-door canvassing costs a campaign considerably more per voter reached than mailed advertising does.
The candidates whose campaigns reached fewer households spent more, on average, on television advertising.
In neighboring cities' council races last year, the link between canvassing and winning was weaker.
Volunteers flock to campaigns already leading in early polls, and the number of households a campaign visits depends mainly on its volunteer count.
questions.explanation: (E) shows the correlation could run backward: candidates already favored to win attract volunteers, and volunteers are what let a campaign reach many households, so being a frontrunner explains both the canvassing and the wins. (D) is tempting, but a weaker link elsewhere is still a link and says nothing about why it held here. (C) actually strengthens by ruling out greater spending as the explanation, and (A) is already built into the 15-of-20 figure.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Canvassing substantially improves a candidate's chances of winning.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. Heavy canvassers: 15 wins out of 20; 2. light canvassers: 6 wins out of 30.

breakdown.analysis: Did knocking on doors make them win, or were the likely winners just the ones who could knock on more doors? That's correlation vs. causation, the most common flaw on the test, and here the risk is reversed causation. We need an answer showing that being a frontrunner produces heavy canvassing, so the canvassing numbers are a symptom, not the cause.

choices.note: So? Five of the 20 heavy canvassers lost; we already knew that. Losing big doesn't change the 75% vs. 20% gap.
Wrong dimension. Cost-effectiveness isn't whether canvassing helps you win.
Opposite. If the light canvassers outspent them on TV and still lost, money isn't the hidden explanation. That helps the strategist.
Tempting. It sounds like the link isn't solid. But 'weaker' still means a link, and other cities don't tell us what caused the pattern here.

CORRECT. Leading candidates attract volunteers; volunteers drive household counts. So frontrunner status → more canvassing, and frontrunner status → winning. The canvassing could be along for the ride.

questions.stimulus: Any city whose transit system runs trains at least every ten minutes during rush hour will see its rush-hour ridership rise. Rush-hour train ridership in Dunmore has been rising steadily. So Dunmore's trains must be running at least every ten minutes during rush hour.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Any museum that offers free admission on weekends will see its weekend attendance rise. Weekend attendance at the Corbin Museum has not risen. So the Corbin Museum must not be offering free admission on weekends.

No bakery whose sourdough starter is over ten years old fails to draw a line of customers before it opens. Hollis Bakery draws a line of customers before it opens. So Hollis Bakery's sourdough starter must be over ten years old.
Every hospital in the region that adopted electronic charts last year reduced its paperwork costs. So electronic charts will reduce paperwork costs at any hospital that adopts them.
Any software team that writes tests for every change will catch most bugs before release. The Ridley team writes tests for every change. So the Ridley team will catch most bugs before release.
Most candidates endorsed by the Ledger newspaper win their elections. Pelham has been endorsed by the Ledger. So Pelham will certainly win the election.
questions.explanation: The argument has the form: frequent trains → rising ridership; ridership is rising; so trains are frequent, which affirms the consequent. (B)'s double-negative premise ('no bakery whose starter is old fails to draw a line') just means old starter → line, and it then infers the old starter from the line, which is the same error. (A) is the trap: it looks closest on the surface but reasons validly by contrapositive (no rise → no free admission), so it isn't flawed at all. (D) is also valid, while (C) and (E) commit different errors.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Dunmore's trains run at least every ten minutes at rush hour.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. Trains every ≤10 min → ridership rises; 2. Dunmore's ridership is rising.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A → B; B; so A. (Affirming the consequent: treats a sufficient condition as if it were necessary.)

breakdown.analysis: So ridership is rising. Can't that happen for a hundred other reasons, like new housing near the stations or higher gas prices? Sure. The rule says frequent trains are one way to get rising ridership, not the only way. This is the classic sufficient/necessary mix-up (affirming the consequent); know it. We need a choice that has A → B, sees B, and concludes A. Careful: the right answer may hide the conditional in odd wording, and a trap may use the valid contrapositive.

choices.note: Tempting. Same 'any X will see a rise' wording, so it looks like a twin. But it goes: free admission → rise; no rise; so no free admission. That's the contrapositive, which is valid. A valid argument can't match a flawed one.
CORRECT. Decode the double negative: 'no old-starter bakery fails to draw a line' = old starter → line. Then: there's a line, so the starter is old. A → B; B; so A. Same flaw, disguised.
Different flaw: a generalization from last year's adopters in one region to every hospital that ever adopts. No conditional is reversed.
Valid: tests → catch most bugs; Ridley tests; so Ridley catches most bugs. A → B; A; so B. No flaw to match.
Different flaw: 'most' becomes 'certainly.' That's treating a probability as a sure thing, not reversing a conditional.

questions.stimulus: Tech lead: More than half of the engineers at Tallis Software work on the mobile app team, and more than half of Tallis's engineers voted in favor of switching to a four-day workweek. So a majority of the engineers on the mobile app team must have voted in favor of the switch.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the tech lead's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: overlooks the possibility that some of Tallis's engineers did not vote on the proposal at all
takes for granted that because most engineers favored the switch, the switch would benefit the company
fails to consider that the engineers who did not vote for the switch could be concentrated on the mobile app team
overlooks the possibility that none of the engineers on the mobile app team voted in favor of the switch
relies on figures about the company as a whole to draw a conclusion about every engineer on the mobile app team
questions.explanation: Two majorities of the same group must overlap, but only by a little: with 100 engineers, 51 on mobile and 51 in favor, all 49 non-supporters could be on mobile, leaving just 2 mobile supporters. (C) names exactly this. (D) is the trap: it describes something impossible, since two majorities of one group must share at least one member. (E) misstates the conclusion, which concerns a majority of the mobile team, not every engineer on it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most mobile-team engineers voted for the four-day week.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 1. More than half of all engineers are on the mobile team; 2. more than half of all engineers voted for the switch.

breakdown.analysis: Two majorities of the same company. Do they have to be mostly the same people? No. They must overlap, but maybe barely. Try 100 engineers: 51 on mobile, 51 yes votes. Put all 49 non-yes engineers on mobile: mobile = 49 non-yes + 2 yes. Mobile majority: no. 'Most' isn't 'most of every part': the yes voters you care about could be the other ones. Hard to prephrase in abstract terms; look for the answer that puts the non-supporters on the mobile team.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The premise already says more than half of all engineers voted yes. Non-voters are just part of the 'not yes' group, and the flaw exists either way.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: 60% of the votes cast were yes, so 60% of all members support the plan.

choices.note: Adds a consequence the argument never mentions. The tech lead says nothing about whether the switch helps the company.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most staff want the switch, so it must be good for the business.

choices.note: CORRECT. Pack the non-supporters onto the mobile team and the overlap can shrink to a sliver. The facts allow a mobile team where most voted no.

Tempting. It sounds like the right worry about a weak overlap. But it's impossible: two groups that each hold more than half of the same company must share someone, so at least one mobile engineer voted yes. The argument can't be faulted for ignoring an impossibility.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The store advertised that every item was on sale, so I assumed my jacket was discounted, overlooking that the clerk might have charged full price.

choices.note: Too strong a reading. The conclusion is about a majority of the mobile team, not every engineer on it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most of the company favors the switch, so every engineer on each team favors it.

passages.title: Constructed editions of unfinished novels
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Passage A

When a novelist dies leaving a book unfinished, her editors face a choice. Increasingly, they have resolved it by producing what might be called a constructed edition: a single continuous reading text assembled from the surviving drafts, with the editor choosing among competing versions of each scene and supplying bridges where the drafts break off. However well intentioned, the practice raises three serious problems.

First, it attributes to the author decisions she never made. When Ilse Varga died in 1961, she left three drafts of The Lantern Year that disagree about the order of its last chapters and even about the fate of its narrator. The 1964 edition settles both questions, and it does so in Varga’s name: the title page announces a novel by Varga, not a novel arranged by her editor.

Second, the constructed edition hides its own seams. Because readers are given a smooth text, they cannot tell which features of the book are the author’s and which are the editor’s. Critics have praised the abrupt, splintered final chapter of The Lantern Year as Varga’s boldest experiment, yet that chapter was spliced together from fragments of two drafts written eleven years apart.

Third, a constructed edition, once published, tends to become the work itself. Teachers assign it, translators work from it, and later scholars who return to the manuscripts find their alternative arrangements treated as curiosities. An editor’s provisional judgment thus hardens into a permanent text. A responsible edition would instead present the drafts as drafts, letting readers see the unfinished work for what it is.

Passage B

Critics of editions that assemble a readable text from a dead writer’s drafts often speak as though the only honest alternative were to publish the drafts themselves, every cancelled line and marginal query preserved. Such editions have real value, but almost no one reads them except specialists. A novel that survives only as a facsimile of its manuscripts survives, for most readers, in name alone.

Nor is it clear that a reading edition takes greater liberties than ordinary publishing does. Even a novel its author saw through the press reflects choices made by others: editors who proposed cuts, copy editors who regularized spelling and punctuation, typesetters whose errors went uncorrected. We do not conclude from this that such novels are not really their authors’ work. A reading edition differs from them in degree, not in kind.

Moreover, a careful editor need not conceal anything. When Tomas Reinholt’s unfinished Salt Roads appeared in 1972, its editor printed an afterword that identified every passage she had moved or bridged and listed the principal variants she had set aside. Readers who wish to know where the author ends and the editor begins can find out; readers who wish simply to read the novel can do that too.

Scholars who would publish nothing but the drafts mistake reverence for the manuscript for fidelity to the writer. Reinholt did not write Salt Roads to be studied in fragments; he wrote it to be read. An edition that lets it be read, and says plainly how it was made, serves his purpose better than one that preserves every crossed-out word.

passages.title: Double couplets in Lake Tarnholm
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
In many lakes fed by glacial meltwater, sediment accumulates on the lake floor in annual bands called varves. Each summer, meltwater carries silt and sand into the lake, where the coarse particles settle quickly into a pale layer; in winter, when ice seals the lake and inflow nearly stops, fine clay settles slowly into a thin dark layer above it. Because each pale-and-dark pair, or couplet, normally represents one year, geologists can date sediment at any depth by counting couplets down from the surface. Lake Tarnholm, in a glaciated mountain valley, seems to defy this method. Cores from its floor contain about 4,100 couplets above the gravel left when the valley’s ice retreated, yet radiocarbon dating of leaf fragments in the lowest sediment indicates that the lake is only about 2,050 years old.

Some researchers concluded that the radiocarbon dates must be in error. But the geologist Ines Haldor points out that the most common source of radiocarbon error in lake sediment—carbon from ancient limestone dissolved in the water—makes samples appear older than they are, not younger, and in any case does not affect leaves, which take their carbon from the air. Haldor proposes instead that the couplet count is right but its interpretation is wrong. Tarnholm, she argues, receives two separate floods of sediment each year. The first comes in late spring, when snow melts on the low slopes around the lake; the second comes in late summer, when the small glacier at the head of the valley reaches its peak melt. Between them, inflow slackens for several weeks and fine clay settles, so each flood leaves its own couplet.

The strongest evidence for Haldor’s view comes from a band of volcanic ash in the cores. The ash has been chemically matched to an eruption of Mount Ossel that, according to regional monastery chronicles, occurred 1,140 years before the cores were taken. If each couplet represented one year, the ash would lie beneath about 1,140 couplets; it lies beneath 2,281, almost exactly two per year. Below the ash, the same ratio holds: the remaining 1,819 couplets span the 910 years between the lake’s formation and the eruption.
