A doubling that persists both above and below the ash is difficult to attribute to any single episode, such as a century of unusual floods.

The couplets also differ as Haldor’s hypothesis predicts. The low slopes around Tarnholm are underlain by dark slate, while the bedrock beneath the glacier is a pale granite rich in feldspar. In the cores, couplets with feldspar-rich coarse layers alternate regularly with couplets whose coarse layers are mostly slate fragments. And at nearby Lake Vessel, in a valley without a glacier, the couplet count and the radiocarbon age agree within a few decades. Haldor’s account does not yet explain why a handful of intervals in the cores contain single rather than double couplets, though she suggests these may record years in which a cool summer kept the glacier from melting enough to send a distinct flood downstream.

passages.title: Velk and the industry theory of adverse possession
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Under the law of Aldmere, a person who openly occupies another’s land without permission for an unbroken period of fifteen years acquires title to it, and the record owner’s claim is extinguished. Lawyers have long found the rule awkward to defend, since it appears to reward trespass. In Land and Labor (1998), the legal scholar Teodora Velk offered what has become the most influential justification for it. The doctrine, she argued, is not a concession to wrongdoers but a reward for industry: land is scarce, and the law transfers it from those who leave it idle to those who put it to use. On this view, the fifteen-year period measures not the owner’s patience but the possessor’s investment, and the possessor’s state of mind—whether she believed the land was hers or knew that it was not—is beside the point.

What Velk fails to clarify is what counts as use. The Aldmere courts have awarded title to possessors who did little more than fence a meadow and graze a few sheep on it, yet they denied title to a possessor who had planted and tended an orchard on a neighbor’s hillside for sixteen years, on the ground that the orchard could not be seen from the public road. If industry were what the doctrine rewards, the orchard grower’s claim would have been the stronger one. Velk’s theory cannot explain why visibility, rather than productivity, so often decides such cases.

The theory also relies on two assumptions that Velk does not defend. The first is that an owner who leaves land unused is neglecting it. Yet some owners leave land unused deliberately—to let a woodland regenerate, to protect a watershed, or to hold it for a later generation—and Velk’s account treats such restraint as the same failing as indifference. The second is that productive use by a possessor is generally more valuable than whatever the owner would eventually have done with the land. That assumption may hold for abandoned farmland, but it is hardly self-evident for land whose owner had plans that the possessor merely anticipated.

Finally, the theory has difficulty with the doctrine’s treatment of owners who are unable to act. Aldmere law suspends the fifteen-year period while the owner is a minor or is legally incapacitated, so that a possessor’s industry, however great, counts for nothing during those years. Velk regards these exceptions as anomalies that a reformed law should abolish. But exceptions that turn entirely on the owner’s capacity to object suggest that the doctrine is concerned at least as much with the owner’s failure to assert a claim as with the possessor’s labor. A theory that must declare a doctrine’s settled features to be mistakes has, to that extent, ceased to describe the doctrine and begun to replace it.

passages.title: Maranho and the telegraph in the Torrin Valley
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
For most of the nineteenth century, the farming districts of the Torrin Valley suffered periodic subsistence crises. When a local harvest failed, grain prices in the affected district could triple within weeks, and deaths from hunger and associated disease rose sharply. After 1880 such crises became far less deadly, and historians long credited the change to hardier seed varieties introduced in the 1870s, which were thought to have made harvests less likely to fail in the first place.

In a 1994 study, the economic historian Ilse Maranho argued that this explanation overlooked a striking pattern. Harvest failures did not become notably rarer after 1880; what changed was their consequences, and the change came first to districts whose market towns had been connected to the telegraph. Maranho’s explanation turned on information. Before the telegraph, a merchant in a well-supplied district learned of a shortage elsewhere only when travelers brought the news, often after prices there had peaked and the worst of the crisis had passed. Once price reports could be sent in hours, merchants could ship grain toward a district as soon as its prices began to rise. Their shipments, Maranho argued, kept prices from climbing to levels at which the poorest households could no longer buy food. As evidence, she showed that the gap between grain prices in connected towns narrowed sharply after each town gained a telegraph office, while the gap among unconnected towns did not.

The thesis drew two objections. Some critics noted that many of the connected towns also acquired rail links in the same decade, and argued that cheaper transport, not faster news, accounted for the narrowing. Others doubted that merchants would behave as Maranho supposed, contending that traders who knew of a shortage might as readily withhold grain to drive prices higher. Maranho answered the first objection by pointing to six towns that had telegraph offices for at least seven years before any railway reached them; in each, the price gap narrowed when the telegraph arrived, not when the railway did. The second objection she could answer only by appeal to the price data themselves, which seemed to her to show that whatever withholding occurred did not prevail.

The discovery in 2009 of the business records of the Brask trading house, a grain firm with agents in eleven valley towns, allowed merchant conduct to be examined directly. The records show agents ordering shipments within two or three days of telegraphed reports of rising prices, and they contain no instance of the firm holding back stock in response to such a report. But they also reveal something Maranho had not anticipated: in towns where the firm’s agents could not obtain credit from a local bank, telegraphed reports of shortages elsewhere produced few shipments, and prices in those towns behaved much as they had before the telegraph. Information, it appears, reduced the toll of harvest failures only where merchants had the means to act on it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following pairs of titles would most likely be found on documents whose relationship to each other is most analogous to the relationship between passage A and passage B?
choices: “Rebuilding the Past: In Defense of Temple Reconstruction” and “Three Objections to Reconstructing Ruined Temples”
“Three Objections to Reconstructing Ruined Temples” and “How Archaeologists Decide Which Temples to Reconstruct”
“Three Objections to Reconstructing Ruined Temples” and “Why Temple Reconstruction Should Be Halted”
“Three Objections to Reconstructing Ruined Temples” and “Rebuilding the Past: In Defense of Temple Reconstruction”
“Rebuilding the Past: In Defense of Temple Reconstruction” and “Temple Reconstruction: A Reply to My Critics”
questions.explanation: Passage A lists three problems with constructed editions; passage B then defends that same practice. D matches that order: a three-objection critique followed by a defense. A is the tempting trap, with the right two kinds of document in the reverse order. B pairs the critique with a neutral how-to, C pairs two critiques, and E pairs two defenses.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the pair of titles that relate to each other the way A relates to B.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of each passage and A’s “First… Second… Third” structure.

breakdown.analysis: Label each passage before you look at the choices. A: “three serious problems” with constructed editions, a critique. B: answers those worries and concludes that a reading edition “serves his purpose better,” a defense. So you want critique first, defense second, same practice. Order matters here; the stem asks about A then B.

choices.note: Right ingredients, wrong order. This is defense then critique. Passage A is the critique, so it has to come first. Classic reversal trap.
The second document is a neutral procedural piece. Passage B isn’t describing how editors work; it argues the practice is worth doing.
Two critiques. Passage B doesn’t pile on; it pushes back.
CORRECT. A numbered critique of a practice followed by a defense of that same practice. That’s exactly A then B.
Two defenses, and the second one is a reply to named critics. Passage B never names A, and A isn’t a defense at all.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: editions that reproduce a writer’s drafts in full have value for scholars
a reading text assembled by an editor from an author’s drafts can legitimately be presented as that author’s work
the editor of an unfinished novel must sometimes choose among conflicting versions of a scene
a constructed edition, once published, tends to become the text that teachers and translators rely on
general readers are more likely to read a smooth reading text than an edition of an author’s drafts
questions.explanation: Passage A objects that the constructed edition attributes to the author decisions she never made, citing a title page that presents the book as Varga’s; passage B replies that outside hands shape every published novel and that a reading edition differs ‘in degree, not in kind,’ so it remains the author’s work. That is B. D is the most tempting trap, but it is A’s third point and passage B never addresses it. A is something both accept, C is common ground, and E is asserted only by passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim where one author would say yes and the other would say no.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: A’s second paragraph (attribution problem) and B’s second paragraph (“degree, not in kind”).

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one author has to take a side and the other has to take the opposite side. Silence doesn’t count. A says the 1964 edition wrongly presents the editor’s choices “in Varga’s name.” B says editorial input doesn’t stop a book from being “really their authors’ work.” That’s a direct clash over attribution.

choices.note: Both would agree. B says outright that such editions “have real value,” and A wants drafts presented as drafts. No conflict.
CORRECT. A: no, the title page falsely credits Varga with the editor’s decisions. B: yes, outside choices shape every published book, and a reading edition differs only in degree. One yes, one no.
Both describe editors choosing among drafts as part of the job. That’s shared background, not a dispute.
Tempting, because it’s A’s third objection. But B never says a word about the reading edition becoming canonical. B is silent, and silence isn’t disagreement.
Only B makes this point (facsimiles are read only by specialists). A never denies it. A’s complaint is about honesty, not readership.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage A would be most likely to offer regarding the suggestion in passage B that an afterword identifying the editor’s changes lets readers know ‘where the author ends and the editor begins’?
choices: An afterword that lists only the principal variants will inevitably leave some of the author’s alternatives unrecorded.
Readers who consult such an afterword will come to prefer the drafts to the reading text.
An afterword is itself an editorial intervention and so is no more trustworthy than the reading text it describes.
An afterword, like an edition of the drafts, is unlikely to be read by anyone except specialists.
Disclosing the editor’s choices does not prevent the editor’s arrangement from becoming the version on which later readers, teachers, and translators rely.
questions.explanation: Passage B’s afterword answers A’s second objection (hidden seams) but not A’s third: that a constructed edition ‘tends to become the work itself’ as teachers assign it and translators work from it. A’s author could therefore say that disclosure leaves the editor’s provisional arrangement just as likely to harden into the permanent text, which is E. A is the strongest trap because B mentions only ‘principal variants,’ but passage A never complains about incomplete lists of variants; its concern is with the arrangement presented as the text. C and D attribute to A claims it never makes, and B is unsupported.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the objection A’s author would raise against B’s afterword fix.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: B’s third paragraph (the Salt Roads afterword) against A’s second and third problems.

breakdown.analysis: Map B’s fix onto A’s three problems. The afterword is aimed at Problem 2: hidden seams. Now ask what it leaves untouched. Problem 3 says the constructed edition becomes the work itself: teachers assign it, translators use it. An afterword does nothing about that. The arrangement still becomes the standard text, footnotes or not. It’s like putting a disclaimer on a map you know is a guess. People still use the map as if it were the real coastline.

choices.note: The big trap. B does say “principal variants,” so this sounds sharp. But A never complains about incomplete variant lists. A’s worries are about attribution, hidden seams, and the arrangement hardening into the standard text. This criticism comes from you, not from A.
Pure speculation. Nothing in A predicts how afterword readers would feel, and if anything A would welcome this outcome.

A never questions an editor’s honesty in describing changes. Its problem is with presenting the editor’s arrangement as the author’s book. Calling the afterword untrustworthy is a new attack A never makes.
Wrong party. The “only specialists read it” point is B’s argument about facsimiles. A never says who reads afterwords.

CORRECT. This is A’s third problem aimed straight at B’s fix: even with full disclosure, the editor’s provisional judgment “hardens into a permanent text” because people assign it, translate it, and treat it as the work.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A argues that a practice is objectionable on several grounds; passage B defends that practice, responding to some but not all of the concerns raised in passage A.
Passage A argues that a practice is objectionable on several grounds; passage B defends that practice, answering each of the objections raised in passage A.
Passage A traces the history of a practice; passage B evaluates the practice in light of that history.
Passage A argues that a practice is objectionable on several grounds; passage B proposes an alternative practice that avoids the problems passage A identifies.
Both passages criticize a practice, but they object to it on different grounds.
questions.explanation: Passage B defends constructed editions and answers two of A’s worries—attribution (outside hands shape every book) and concealment (an afterword can disclose the changes)—but never responds to A’s third, that such an edition hardens into the standard text. So A is correct. B is the trap: it is identical except that it claims B answers every objection. D misreads B, which defends the same practice rather than proposing an alternative, and C and E misdescribe one passage or the other.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how B relates to A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Line up A’s three problems against B’s paragraphs 2–4.

breakdown.analysis: Make a scorecard. Problem 1 (credit goes to the author for the editor’s decisions): B answers it in paragraph 2, since all publishing involves other hands. Problem 2 (hidden seams): B answers it in paragraph 3 with the afterword. Problem 3 (the edition becomes the standard text): B never addresses it. So B defends the practice and answers two of three. When two choices differ by one word like “some” vs. “each,” check that word against the passage.

choices.note: CORRECT. A critiques on several grounds; B defends the same practice and answers two of the three worries, skipping the “hardens into a permanent text” point. “Some but not all” is exactly right.
Almost identical to A, but “each” is too strong. B never responds to the third problem, that the edition becomes the work itself. One unanswered objection kills this choice.
A isn’t a history. It’s a critique with numbered problems. The dates (1961, 1964) are examples, not a narrative of how the practice developed.

B doesn’t propose an alternative. It defends the very practice A attacks: assembling a reading text, plus disclosure. The afterword is a way of doing the same thing carefully, not a different practice.
B doesn’t criticize the practice; it defends it. The only people B criticizes are the purists.

questions.stem: The author of passage B suggests that some scholars are too
choices: permissive
careless
reverent
credulous
cynical
questions.explanation: Passage B’s last paragraph says that scholars who would publish nothing but the drafts ‘mistake reverence for the manuscript for fidelity to the writer’: their devotion to the physical drafts is excessive, so C is correct. A and B point the wrong way, since these scholars are faulted for being overly strict, not lax. D and E have no basis in the passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Fill in the one word for B’s complaint about some scholars.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last paragraph of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: Find who B criticizes: “scholars who would publish nothing but the drafts.” Their fault is that they “mistake reverence for the manuscript for fidelity to the writer.” They care too much about every crossed-out word. Prephrase: too worshipful of the paper. That’s “reverent.”

choices.note: Opposite. These scholars are too strict, not too lax. They won’t let an editor touch anything.
Also opposite. They preserve “every crossed-out word.” That’s the opposite of careless.
CORRECT. B says they mistake “reverence for the manuscript” for fidelity. Too much reverence is the whole charge.
Credulous means too ready to believe things. B never says these scholars believe anything naively.
Social-autopilot trap. Nothing in B suggests the scholars are cynical about anyone’s motives. Their problem is excess devotion.

questions.stem: The author of passage A mentions critics’ praise for the final chapter of The Lantern Year (second sentence of the third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that critics have generally misjudged Varga’s achievement as a novelist
illustrate how undisclosed editorial intervention can lead readers to attribute to an author a feature of a text that the author did not create
suggest that Varga intended The Lantern Year to end in a deliberately fragmentary way
provide evidence that a constructed edition comes to be treated as the definitive version of a work
argue that the drafts of The Lantern Year should be published in the order in which they were written
questions.explanation: The example sits under A’s second problem, that a constructed edition ‘hides its own seams’ so readers cannot tell the author’s features from the editor’s. Critics credited Varga with a bold experiment that was in fact the editor’s splice, which is B. D is the tempting trap, but the canonization of the edition is A’s third problem, and this example illustrates the second. A overgeneralizes, C contradicts the example, and E is a proposal the passage never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Why does A bring up the critics who praised the final chapter?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph (“Second, the constructed edition hides its own seams”).

breakdown.analysis: Ask which point the example sits under. It’s in Problem 2: readers can’t tell the author’s parts from the editor’s. Critics praised the splintered chapter as “Varga’s boldest experiment,” but it was spliced from two drafts eleven years apart. So the example shows hidden editing fooling readers into crediting the author. Examples on the LSAT almost always serve the claim right next to them.

choices.note: Too broad. The example is about one chapter, not Varga’s whole career, and A doesn’t say critics are generally wrong about her.
CORRECT. Critics credited Varga with a feature the editor created by splicing. That’s Problem 2 in action: hidden seams lead to misattribution.
Opposite. A’s point is that Varga didn’t design that ending; it was stitched together after her death.
Wrong problem. “Becomes the definitive version” is Problem 3, in the next paragraph. This example shows misattribution, not canonization.
A never proposes publishing the drafts in chronological order. It says only that a responsible edition would “present the drafts as drafts.”

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Editions that reproduce an author’s drafts in full should no longer be published.
A reading edition of an unfinished novel is justified only if the author left instructions for completing it.
Copy editors generally take greater liberties with a text than do the editors of reading editions.
Readers of a reading edition are generally unaware that its text was assembled by an editor.
That people other than the author helped shape a published text does not by itself make the text something other than the author’s work.
questions.explanation: In its second paragraph passage B notes that editors, copy editors, and typesetters shape even novels their authors saw through the press, yet ‘we do not conclude’ that such novels are not their authors’ work—which is E. A is too extreme, since B grants that draft editions ‘have real value.’ C goes beyond B, which says only that it is ‘not clear’ a reading edition takes greater liberties, not that it takes fewer. D conflicts with B’s point that an afterword can tell readers how the text was made, and B is never suggested.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement B’s author would endorse.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph, plus the afterword in the third.

breakdown.analysis: B’s key move is the analogy to ordinary publishing: every published novel bears marks of editors, copy editors, typesetters, “we do not conclude from this that such novels are not really their authors’ work.” Prephrase: outside help doesn’t by itself strip authorship. Then look for the choice that says that.

choices.note: Too extreme. B says draft editions “have real value.” B just doesn’t think they should be the only option.
Made-up condition. B never mentions author instructions. Reinholt’s edition is defended without any.
Goes too far. B says only that it’s “not clear” a reading edition takes greater liberties than ordinary publishing. Not sure X is bigger than Y doesn’t mean Y is bigger than X.
B’s point is the opposite: a careful edition “need not conceal anything,” and readers can find out how it was made.
CORRECT. This is B’s second paragraph in general form: outside hands shape every book, but that alone doesn’t make the book someone else’s.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The apparent conflict between the couplet count and the radiocarbon age of Lake Tarnholm’s sediment is best explained by the hypothesis that the lake receives two distinct floods of sediment each year, a hypothesis supported by several lines of evidence.
The radiocarbon dates for Lake Tarnholm’s sediment must be mistaken, since the couplet count shows that the lake is about 4,100 years old.
Counting couplets is an unreliable method of dating lake sediment, as the conflicting evidence from Lake Tarnholm demonstrates.
Ash from an eruption of Mount Ossel provides the most reliable means of dating the sediment of lakes in Lake Tarnholm’s region.
Lake Tarnholm’s sediment contains two kinds of couplets, one derived from slate and the other from granite, because the lake’s catchment includes two types of bedrock.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the mismatch between 4,100 couplets and a 2,050-year radiocarbon age, gives Haldor’s two-floods-a-year explanation, and then lays out the ash and bedrock evidence for it, as A says. B is the view Haldor rejects. C overgeneralizes, since Lake Vessel shows the method working where there is one flood a year. D and E are supporting details, not the main point.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: State the passage’s main point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First and last sentences of each paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Structure: puzzle (twice as many couplets as years), then Haldor’s theory (two floods a year), then the evidence (ash ratio, slate/granite alternation, Lake Vessel). The main point has to cover the puzzle and the theory, and say the evidence supports it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Puzzle, theory, and support, all in one sentence. That’s the passage.
This is the view Haldor rejects in the second paragraph. The radiocarbon age is right; the couplet count is just being read wrong.
Too broad. The method works fine at Lake Vessel. Only the one-couplet-per-year assumption fails at Tarnholm.
One piece of evidence, blown up into a superlative (“most reliable”) for a whole region. Way too narrow and too strong.
True detail from paragraph four, but it leaves out the puzzle and the theory. It’s supporting evidence, not the point.

questions.stem: In saying that the couplet count is right ‘but its interpretation is wrong’ (middle of the second paragraph), Haldor most likely means that
choices: some couplets in the cores were overlooked because they are too thin to distinguish
the radiocarbon ages have been taken to date the lake when they in fact date only the leaves
the couplets in the Tarnholm cores were formed by processes other than the melting of snow and ice
the number of couplets has been accurately determined, but the assumption that each couplet records a single year does not hold at Tarnholm
geologists have wrongly assumed that couplets can be used to date the sediment of any lake
questions.explanation: The ‘interpretation’ in question is the standard reading set out in the first paragraph, that each couplet represents one year. Haldor keeps the count of about 4,100 but argues that Tarnholm gets two floods, and so two couplets, every year, which is D. A contradicts ‘the couplet count is right.’ B shifts the error to the radiocarbon dates, which Haldor defends. C contradicts her theory, since both floods are meltwater, and E overgeneralizes beyond Tarnholm.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what Haldor means by “count right, interpretation wrong.”

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, read against the first paragraph’s rule that “each… couplet… normally represents one year.”

breakdown.analysis: Two parts: the count (about 4,100 couplets) and what the count is taken to mean (one couplet = one year). Haldor keeps the first and rejects the second: two floods a year, so two couplets a year. 4,100 ÷ 2 = 2,050, which matches the radiocarbon age.

choices.note: Contradicts the phrase itself. Haldor says the count is right. If couplets had been missed, the count would be wrong, and it would make the gap worse anyway.
Wrong target. Haldor defends the radiocarbon dates. The “interpretation” is of the couplet count, not the dates.
Both floods are melt: snow in spring, glacier in summer. Haldor’s theory needs melting to be the cause.
CORRECT. The 4,100 count stands; what fails is the one-couplet-per-year reading. At Tarnholm it’s two per year.
Too broad. Lake Vessel shows the usual method works where there’s one flood a year. Haldor’s point is about Tarnholm.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the most common source of radiocarbon error in lake sediment
choices: affects leaf fragments more strongly than other organic material
accounts for the discrepancy between the Tarnholm couplet count and the radiocarbon age
tends to make samples appear older than they actually are
results from carbon released into lakes by volcanic eruptions
has been shown to be absent from Lake Tarnholm’s water
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says this error, caused by carbon from ancient limestone, ‘makes samples appear older than they are, not younger.’ That is C. B is the trap: the error runs the wrong way to explain why the radiocarbon age is younger than the couplet count suggests. A reverses the passage, which says leaves are unaffected, D swaps limestone for volcanoes, and E is never stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage actually says about the usual radiocarbon error.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Read the line: old limestone carbon “makes samples appear older than they are, not younger, and… does not affect leaves.” That’s why it can’t rescue the critics: their story needs the dates to be too young, and this error pushes them older. Detail questions reward the exact line, not the general vibe.

choices.note: Reversed. The passage says this error does not affect leaves, because leaves take their carbon from the air.
Tempting, but it runs the wrong way. The radiocarbon age is younger than the couplets imply. An error that makes samples look older would widen the gap, not explain it.
CORRECT. Straight from the second paragraph: it makes samples appear “older than they are, not younger.”
Mixes up two parts of the passage. The error comes from dissolved limestone. Volcanic ash shows up only as a date marker.
Never said. The passage says the error doesn’t affect leaves, not that it’s missing from the lake.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: describe the method by which geologists ordinarily date the sediment of glacial lakes
offer an alternative to the explanation proposed in the second paragraph
show that the radiocarbon dates discussed in the first paragraph are unreliable
explain why some intervals in the Tarnholm cores contain single rather than double couplets
use an independently dated marker to show that a pattern predicted by a hypothesis holds in more than one portion of the sediment record
questions.explanation: The third paragraph uses the Mount Ossel ash, dated by chronicles, to show two couplets per year both above the ash (2,281 couplets in 1,140 years) and below it (1,819 in 910). That supports Haldor’s two-floods-a-year hypothesis and rules out a one-time episode, which is E. C is the main trap, but the ash confirms the radiocarbon timeline rather than undermining it. A describes the first paragraph, D the end of the fourth, and B wrongly treats the paragraph as a rival theory.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what the ash paragraph does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, checked against the second (the theory) and fourth (more evidence).

breakdown.analysis: Do the arithmetic yourself. Above the ash: 2,281 couplets ÷ 1,140 years ≈ 2.0. Below: 1,819 ÷ 910 ≈ 2.0. Together they add up to 4,100 couplets in 2,050 years. Haldor predicts two a year, and the ash shows it in both halves of the core. That’s why the last sentence says it can’t be “a century of unusual floods.” So the paragraph is evidence for the theory, and it shows the ratio holds throughout.

choices.note: That’s the first paragraph’s job. The third paragraph is about a specific ash layer at Tarnholm.
No new theory appears. The ash paragraph supports Haldor’s view; it calls itself “the strongest evidence” for it.
Opposite. The chronicle date agrees with the two-per-year rate, and so with the 2,050-year radiocarbon age. The ash backs up the radiocarbon dates.
That’s the last sentence of the passage, in paragraph four.
CORRECT. The ash is dated independently, by chronicles. The doubling it shows appears both above and below it. That’s a predicted pattern holding in two portions of the record.

questions.stem: If Haldor’s suggestion about the intervals that contain single rather than double couplets (last sentence of the passage) is correct, which one of the following would most likely be true of the couplets in those intervals?
choices: Their coarse layers would consist mostly of feldspar-rich granite.
Their coarse layers would consist mostly of slate fragments.
They would be thicker than the couplets in the rest of the cores.
They would contain traces of volcanic ash.
They would have formed in years when little snow fell on the slopes around the lake.
questions.explanation: Haldor suggests that in those years a cool summer kept the glacier from sending its flood, so only the spring snowmelt from the low slopes would reach the lake. The fourth paragraph says those slopes are underlain by slate, while the glacier sits on feldspar-rich granite, so the single couplets should be slate-rich, as B says. A reverses the two sources and is the main trap. E blames the wrong season’s melt, and C and D have no basis in the passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict what the single couplets would look like if Haldor’s cool-summer idea is right.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence (cool summer, no glacier flood), the second paragraph (which flood comes from where), and the fourth paragraph (slate slopes, granite under the glacier).

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Cool summer → glacier doesn’t send a flood → only the spring snowmelt flood arrives. Spring flood comes from the low slopes → low slopes are slate → coarse layer is mostly slate. You need three paragraphs for this one; that’s what makes it hard.

choices.note: Reversed. Feldspar-rich granite is the glacier’s signature, and the glacier flood is exactly what’s missing in those years.
CORRECT. With no glacier flood, only the spring snowmelt from the slate slopes delivers coarse sediment, so the coarse layer should be slate.
Nothing in the passage ties these couplets to thickness. You’d have to invent a reason.
The ash is one band from one eruption. Nothing links it to cool summers or single couplets.

Wrong season and wrong source. Haldor blames a cool summer that kept the glacier from melting, not a lack of snow on the slopes. A snowless year would remove the slate flood, the opposite of what she proposes.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Haldor’s hypothesis?
choices: In some lakes far from Lake Tarnholm, couplets are known to form at a rate of more than one per year for reasons unrelated to glaciers.
The monastery chronicles that record the eruption of Mount Ossel also mention several earlier eruptions whose ash has not been found in the Tarnholm cores.
Leaf fragments that reach lake sediment sometimes fell from their trees several years before they were buried.
The glacier at the head of Lake Tarnholm’s valley formed only about 600 years ago, after a long period during which the upper valley was free of ice.
In late spring, meltwater from the slopes around Lake Tarnholm carries more sediment into the lake than the glacier does in late summer.
questions.explanation: Haldor’s hypothesis needs a late-summer glacier flood every year, and the third paragraph shows the two-per-year ratio holding even below the ash, over 1,140 years ago. If the glacier is only about 600 years old, the older sediment could not have formed that way, yet it still shows double couplets, so D seriously undermines the hypothesis. B is the trap, but missing ash from other eruptions does not challenge the match or date of the Ossel ash. A is consistent with the hypothesis, C involves errors far too small to matter, and E is compatible with two floods a year.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages the two-floods-a-year theory.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (the glacier causes the second flood) and third paragraph (the ratio holds below the ash too).

breakdown.analysis: The theory needs a working glacier for the whole 2,050 years, because the doubling runs all the way down the core. So attack the glacier. If it showed up only 600 years ago, the sediment from 600 to 2,050 years ago had no glacier flood. It should have one couplet a year. But the ash math shows two a year below the ash too, more than 1,140 years back. The theory can’t explain that.

choices.note: If anything this helps: it shows multiple couplets a year is possible. And far-off lakes say nothing about what causes Tarnholm’s.

Tempting because it targets the ash evidence. But ash from other eruptions may simply not have reached the lake. It doesn’t touch the match or the date of the Ossel ash, so the 2-per-year arithmetic stands.
A few years of error in a 2,050-year date is trivial. The discrepancy is a factor of two, about 2,000 years.

CORRECT. No glacier before about 600 years ago means no late-summer flood, so the older sediment should have one couplet a year. The core shows two a year below the ash anyway, so Haldor’s mechanism can’t be the cause.
The theory only needs two separate floods, not equal ones. A bigger spring flood fits fine.

questions.stem: The information yielded by which one of the following studies would be most useful in determining whether Haldor’s explanation of the Tarnholm couplets is correct?
choices: Placing sediment traps on the floor of Lake Tarnholm for several years and recording how many coarse layers accumulate each year and which bedrock their particles come from
Radiocarbon dating additional leaf fragments from the lowest sediment of Lake Vessel
Determining the chemical composition of ash from other eruptions of Mount Ossel
Counting the couplets in additional cores taken from the floor of Lake Tarnholm
Measuring how much sediment glaciers in other valleys of the region deliver to lakes in a typical summer
questions.explanation: Haldor’s claim is that Tarnholm gets two floods a year, a slate-rich spring flood and a granite-rich late-summer flood, each leaving its own coarse layer. Watching the sediment build up over several years tests this directly, as A proposes. D is the trap: nobody disputes the couplet count, only how many years each couplet represents. B concerns a different lake whose dates already agree, C does not bear on the timing of the floods, and E looks at other valleys.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the study that would best test the two-floods theory.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (the mechanism) and fourth (slate vs. granite).

breakdown.analysis: What exactly is in dispute? Not the count, and not the radiocarbon date. It’s whether one year at Tarnholm lays down two coarse layers from two sources. The best test watches that happen in real time. It’s like settling whether a bird nests twice a season: you don’t count old nests, you watch one season.

choices.note: CORRECT. Watching Tarnholm’s floor for several years shows directly how many coarse layers form per year and whether they alternate slate and granite. That’s the theory’s prediction.
Lake Vessel’s dates already match its couplets. More dates there tell you nothing new about Tarnholm.
Other Ossel eruptions don’t bear on how many floods Tarnholm gets each year.
The trap. Nobody doubts the count; Haldor says “the couplet count is right.” Counting again can’t tell you what each couplet means.
Other valleys, other lakes. Even if their glaciers deliver a lot, that doesn’t show Tarnholm gets a separate summer flood that leaves its own couplet.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Velk’s industry theory, though influential, should be replaced by an account that makes the possessor’s good faith the decisive consideration.
The courts of Aldmere have applied the adverse possession doctrine inconsistently, rewarding visibility in some cases and productivity in others, so no theory can fit them.
Velk’s view that the doctrine rewards productive use is unclear about what counts as use, rests on undefended assumptions, and fails to fit features of the doctrine.
The adverse possession doctrine of Aldmere cannot be justified, because it rewards trespassers at the expense of owners who leave land unused for good reasons.
Velk is right that the doctrine rewards industry, but she errs in proposing that the exceptions for minors and incapacitated owners be abolished.
questions.explanation: The passage introduces Velk’s industry theory and then criticizes it in three steps: it fails to clarify what counts as use (second paragraph), relies on undefended assumptions (third), and cannot handle the exceptions for owners unable to act (fourth), which is C. E is the most tempting trap, but the author never grants that the doctrine rewards industry; the second paragraph argues that visibility, not productivity, decides cases. D attacks the doctrine itself, whereas the author attacks only Velk’s justification of it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point: the one claim the whole passage is built to support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of each paragraph: P1 presents Velk; P2 ‘fails to clarify’; P3 ‘two assumptions’; P4 ‘Finally... difficulty’.

breakdown.analysis: This is the classic ‘theory, then what it fails to clarify, its assumptions, and its complications’ structure. The author is criticizing Velk’s justification, not the doctrine and not the courts. So the main point should name Velk’s theory and say it falls short, ideally in the three ways the passage lists. Prephrase: Velk’s industry theory doesn’t fit the doctrine well.

choices.note: Wrong. The passage never says good faith should decide anything. Velk calls state of mind ‘beside the point,’ and the author never pushes back on that. This invents a replacement theory.

Wrong. The courts are consistent in the passage’s telling: visibility ‘so often decides such cases.’ The orchard case is evidence against Velk, not a charge of judicial inconsistency. Right topic, wrong target.

CORRECT. It names the target (Velk’s theory) and hits all three criticisms: what counts as use (P2), the undefended assumptions (P3), and the owner-focused exceptions (P4). That’s the whole passage in one sentence.

Wrong. The author criticizes a justification of the doctrine, not the doctrine. In fact P4 suggests the doctrine makes sense as being about the owner’s failure to assert a claim. This is too strong and aims at the wrong thing.

Half-right trap. The author does doubt Velk on the exceptions, but never agrees that the doctrine rewards industry. P2 says the opposite: visibility, not productivity, decides cases. An answer that is half wrong is all wrong.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Velk’s theory can best be described as one of
choices: admiration
contempt
indifference
ambivalence
skepticism
questions.explanation: The author raises objection after objection to Velk’s theory in measured language (‘fails to clarify,’ ‘does not defend,’ ‘has difficulty’), which is skepticism, E. Ambivalence (D) is the tempting trap because the author grants that one assumption ‘may hold for abandoned farmland,’ but that small concession doesn’t balance three paragraphs of criticism. Contempt (B) is far too strong for the passage’s calm tone.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the one word that captures how the author feels about Velk’s theory.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraphs 2–4, especially the verbs: ‘fails to clarify,’ ‘does not defend,’ ‘has difficulty,’ ‘ceased to describe the doctrine.’

breakdown.analysis: Every paragraph after the first is a criticism, but the language is academic and measured. That’s doubt, not hatred. Prephrase: critical, doubtful. On attitude questions, match both direction (negative) and strength (moderate).

choices.note: Wrong direction. Calling the theory ‘the most influential justification’ reports its reputation; it isn’t the author’s praise. The rest of the passage is criticism.

Right direction, too strong. Contempt means scorn. The author never mocks Velk; the tone is careful and specific. Watch for extreme attitude words on RC: the LSAT’s authors are almost never contemptuous.
Wrong. Someone indifferent wouldn’t spend three paragraphs taking the theory apart.

Tempting, but wrong. Ambivalence means real mixed feelings. The only nod to Velk is that one assumption ‘may hold for abandoned farmland,’ and it’s immediately followed by ‘but.’ One small concession doesn’t make the author torn.
CORRECT. The author doubts the theory on three separate grounds and says so calmly. Skepticism is negative but measured, which matches the tone exactly.

questions.stem: The passage raises all of the following as complications for Velk’s theory EXCEPT:
choices: the doctrine’s disregard of whether the possessor believed the land to be her own
the awarding of title to possessors whose activity on the land was slight
the existence of owners who leave land unused for purposes they consider worthwhile
the suspension of the fifteen-year period for owners who are unable to assert their rights
the possibility that an owner’s eventual use of the land would have been more valuable than the possessor’s
questions.explanation: The doctrine’s indifference to the possessor’s state of mind appears in the first paragraph as part of Velk’s own view, and the author never treats it as a problem for her theory, so A is the exception. B (fencing and grazing, second paragraph), C and E (the two assumptions, third paragraph), and D (minority and incapacity, fourth paragraph) are all raised against the theory. A is easy to miss because it is mentioned in the passage; the question asks what is raised as a complication, not what is mentioned.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Four answers are complications the passage raises for Velk’s theory. Find the one that isn’t.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P2 (what counts as use), P3 (two assumptions), P4 (owners unable to act). Also P1, to see what belongs to Velk’s own view.

breakdown.analysis: Make a quick list of the complications: (1) minimal use like fencing and grazing wins title while an unseen orchard loses; (2) some owners leave land unused on purpose; (3) the possessor’s use may not beat the owner’s eventual plans; (4) the period is suspended for minors and incapacitated owners. Anything not on that list is the answer. Careful: an EXCEPT answer can be mentioned in the passage and still not be a complication.

choices.note: CORRECT. The possessor’s state of mind comes up only in P1, as part of Velk’s position (‘beside the point’). The author never says it causes her any trouble. Mentioned, yes; raised as a complication, no.
Raised. P2: courts gave title to possessors who ‘did little more than fence a meadow and graze a few sheep.’ That’s part of the ‘what counts as use’ problem.
Raised. P3’s first assumption: some owners leave land unused ‘deliberately’ to let a woodland regenerate, protect a watershed, or save it for a later generation.
Raised. P4: the period is suspended while the owner is a minor or incapacitated, which the author says points to the owner’s conduct rather than the possessor’s labor.
Raised. P3’s second assumption: that the possessor’s use is more valuable than ‘whatever the owner would eventually have done,’ which the author says isn’t self-evident.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Velk’s position commits her to which one of the following views?
choices: A possessor who knew the land was not hers should be required to occupy it for longer than one who believed it was hers.
Owners who leave land unused in order to let it regenerate should be protected from losing title to possessors.
Land that its owner leaves idle for fifteen years should pass to the state for reassignment to those who will put it to productive use.
Other things being equal, a possessor who has tended an orchard for sixteen years has a stronger claim to title than one who has merely grazed sheep on a meadow.
Whether a possessor’s occupation can be seen from a public road should be decisive in disputes over title.
questions.explanation: Velk holds that the doctrine rewards industry, and the second paragraph says outright that if industry were what the doctrine rewards, the orchard grower’s claim would be the stronger one, so she is committed to D. B is tempting because it echoes the author’s sympathy for deliberate non-use, but that is the author’s complication, not anything Velk’s view requires; her account treats such restraint like indifference. C goes further than her theory, which concerns transfers to possessors who actually use the land, and A contradicts her claim that state of mind is beside the point.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a view Velk has to accept, given what she’s said, whether or not she said it herself.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P1 for Velk’s claims (industry is rewarded; state of mind is beside the point); P2 for the orchard-versus-meadow comparison; P4 for her view of the exceptions.

breakdown.analysis: Velk: the doctrine rewards industry, the period measures the possessor’s investment, and the possessor’s state of mind doesn’t matter. P2 gives you the bridge: ‘If industry were what the doctrine rewards, the orchard grower’s claim would have been the stronger one.’ Velk says industry is exactly what it rewards. So she’s stuck saying the orchard grower should have won. A commitment answer must follow from her view, not just be compatible with it.

choices.note: Opposite. Velk says whether the possessor ‘believed the land was hers or knew that it was not’ is ‘beside the point.’ She can’t then want different periods based on belief.
Wrong party. This is the author’s worry from P3. Velk’s account ‘treats such restraint as the same failing as indifference,’ so if anything she’s committed to the opposite.
Adds a consequence. Velk’s theory is about transferring land to possessors who use it, not about the state seizing idle land. Nothing in her view requires a state-run reassignment scheme.

CORRECT. The orchard grower showed more industry than the sheep grazer. Since Velk says the doctrine rewards industry, she has to say the orchard grower’s claim is stronger, which is exactly what P2 points out. ‘Other things being equal’ keeps it safely narrow.
Opposite. Visibility deciding cases is the courts’ practice that the author says Velk’s theory ‘cannot explain.’ Her theory points to productivity, not visibility.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: present cases in which the courts of Aldmere reached outcomes that Velk’s theory would not predict
identify presuppositions of the theory described in the first paragraph and question whether they hold generally
argue that the doctrine should not apply to land that its owner has left unused deliberately
propose an alternative account of the purpose that the adverse possession doctrine serves
concede that Velk’s theory correctly describes how the doctrine applies to abandoned farmland
questions.explanation: The third paragraph names two assumptions Velk’s theory relies on, that unused land is neglected and that a possessor’s use is worth more than the owner’s, and shows each fails in some cases, which is B. E seizes on the concession that the second assumption ‘may hold for abandoned farmland,’ but that is a passing qualification, not the paragraph’s purpose. C overreaches: the author points out that deliberate non-use complicates the theory but never proposes changing the doctrine.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the third paragraph does in the passage’s argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P3 in full: ‘The theory also relies on two assumptions that Velk does not defend’ and the two examples that follow.

breakdown.analysis: The topic sentence tells you the job: list two unstated assumptions of Velk’s theory, then show each one fails in some cases (deliberate non-use; land whose owner had plans). Prephrase: point out assumptions behind Velk’s view and show they don’t always hold. Function questions are about the paragraph’s main job, not one clause inside it.

choices.note: Wrong paragraph. Court cases (the meadow and the orchard) are P2’s job. P3 contains no cases at all.

CORRECT. ‘Presuppositions’ = the two undefended assumptions; ‘the theory described in the first paragraph’ = Velk’s; ‘question whether they hold generally’ = the woodland and owner’s-plans examples. Abstract wording, but it matches point for point.
Adds a consequence. The author uses deliberate non-use to show Velk’s assumption is shaky, not to propose a reform. The passage never says how the doctrine should change.
Wrong paragraph. The hint of an alternative (the owner’s failure to assert a claim) shows up in P4, not P3.

Half-right trap. P3 does say the second assumption ‘may hold for abandoned farmland,’ but that’s a quick concession on the way to ‘but it is hardly self-evident’ elsewhere. It’s a detail, not the paragraph’s function.

questions.stem: The author mentions the orchard on a neighbor’s hillside (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate a case in which the doctrine produced an outcome contrary to what Velk’s theory would lead one to expect
show that the courts of Aldmere have failed to apply the requirement of visibility consistently
suggest that a possessor’s belief about who owns the land should bear on whether she acquires title
provide an example of an owner who left land unused for a purpose the owner considered worthwhile
support Velk’s claim that the fifteen-year period measures the possessor’s investment in the land
questions.explanation: The orchard grower showed more industry than the meadow possessors yet lost because the orchard couldn’t be seen from the road, so the case cuts against Velk’s claim that the doctrine rewards industry, which is A. B misreads the case: the courts applied visibility, and the author says visibility ‘so often decides’ cases, so the example shows consistency with visibility, not inconsistency. E reverses the example’s role.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author brings up the orchard.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P2, especially the sentence right after the example: ‘If industry were what the doctrine rewards, the orchard grower’s claim would have been the stronger one.’

breakdown.analysis: The orchard is a high-industry possessor who lost; the meadow grazers were low-industry possessors who won. That’s the reverse of what an industry-reward theory predicts. The author tells you this directly in the next sentence. Prephrase: a counterexample to Velk.

choices.note: CORRECT. More industry, no title. Less industry, title. Velk’s theory predicts the opposite, and that’s the whole point of the example.

Wrong. The orchard lost because it couldn’t be seen, which is the visibility rule being applied, not ignored. The author says visibility ‘so often decides’ cases. Nothing here suggests courts are inconsistent about visibility.
Out of scope. The orchard grower’s beliefs are never mentioned, and the author never argues that belief should matter.
Wrong party. The deliberate non-use examples are in P3 (woodland, watershed, later generation). The passage says nothing about why the neighbor wasn’t using the hillside.
Opposite. The example undermines Velk. If the period measured investment, sixteen years of tending an orchard should have earned title.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would be most likely to regard which one of the following as a more promising basis than Velk’s for explaining the adverse possession doctrine of Aldmere?
choices: the value of the improvements that a possessor makes to the land
whether the possessor sincerely believed the land to be her own
the length of time for which the owner has left the land idle
the social value of the uses to which the owner intended to put the land
whether the owner had a fair opportunity to object to the possession and failed to do so
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the minority and incapacity exceptions suggest the doctrine is concerned with ‘the owner’s failure to assert a claim,’ and the visibility requirement in the second paragraph fits the same idea, since an owner can object only to a possession she can see, so E. D is the strongest trap because the third paragraph mentions owners’ plans, but there the point is only that Velk can’t assume a possessor’s use beats them; nothing suggests the doctrine turns on the social value of owners’ plans. C focuses on the owner’s idleness, which the author warns against equating with neglect, and A is essentially Velk’s own view.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer what kind of explanation of the doctrine the author would find better than Velk’s.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P4’s last two sentences (‘the owner’s capacity to object... the owner’s failure to assert a claim’), plus P2’s visibility point.

breakdown.analysis: P4 practically tells you: the exceptions ‘turn entirely on the owner’s capacity to object,’ so the doctrine is about ‘the owner’s failure to assert a claim.’ Now connect P2: visibility decides cases, and an owner can only object to what she can see. Both features fit an ‘owner had a chance to object and didn’t’ account. Combining two paragraphs is how hard RC inferences work.

choices.note: This is basically Velk’s industry theory. The author is looking for something better than it, so this can’t be it.
Out of scope. The possessor’s good faith is mentioned only as something Velk sets aside. The author never suggests it explains visibility or the exceptions.

Tempting, but wrong. Idle time is about the owner’s non-use, and P3 warns that non-use isn’t the same as neglect. It also can’t explain the exceptions: a minor’s land can sit idle for years and the period still doesn’t run.

Strong trap. Owners’ plans do appear in P3, but only to show that Velk can’t assume the possessor’s use is worth more. The author never says the doctrine depends on how valuable those plans are, and this wouldn’t explain visibility or the minority exception.

CORRECT. A fair opportunity to object explains both features Velk can’t: the exceptions (minors and incapacitated owners can’t object) and visibility (you can’t object to an orchard you can’t see). That’s exactly where P4 points.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Contrary to the long-held view, hardier seed varieties played no part in reducing the deadliness of harvest failures in the Torrin Valley after 1880.
Maranho’s view that faster price information made harvest failures less deadly has been largely confirmed, though later evidence shows the effect depended on merchants’ credit.
The narrowing of grain price gaps among Torrin Valley towns after 1880 is better explained by the arrival of railways than by the spread of the telegraph.
The records of the Brask trading house demonstrate that grain merchants in the Torrin Valley did not withhold stock to drive up prices during shortages.
Access to bank credit, rather than access to price information, was what reduced the toll of subsistence crises in the Torrin Valley.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the old seed explanation to Maranho’s telegraph thesis, through the objections, to the Brask records, which confirm her account of merchant behavior while adding that information mattered only where merchants had credit, which is B. E is the tempting trap because it picks up the passage’s final twist, but the last sentence makes credit a condition for information to work, not a replacement for it. D overstates one finding: the records show no withholding by one firm, not by valley merchants generally.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point of the whole passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P2 (Maranho’s thesis), P3 (objections and her replies), and especially P4’s last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Structure: old explanation (seeds) → Maranho’s finding and mechanism (telegraph, merchants ship grain fast) → two objections → new evidence that mostly backs her but adds a condition (credit). Prephrase: Maranho was basically right, with a credit twist. A main point should cover the finding and how later evidence revised it.

choices.note: Too strong. Maranho says harvest failures didn’t become rarer, which undercuts the seed story, but the passage never says seeds had ‘no part’ at all. It also ignores Maranho entirely.
CORRECT. Maranho’s thesis is the center of the passage, the Brask records largely confirm it, and the final paragraph adds the credit condition. This covers the whole arc.
Wrong party. That’s the critics’ objection, which Maranho answered with the six towns. The author never endorses it.
Too broad and too narrow. Too broad because the records come from one firm, not all valley merchants. Too narrow because it leaves out Maranho’s thesis and the credit finding.

Reverses the relationship. The last sentence says information worked ‘only where merchants had the means to act on it.’ Credit is a condition for information to help, not a substitute for it. Both mattered.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about the explanation that historians long gave for the declining deadliness of subsistence crises in the Torrin Valley?
choices: It was abandoned by most historians soon after Maranho’s study appeared.
It attributed the decline chiefly to improvements in the transport of grain.
It was contradicted by the Brask records, which show that harvests failed as often after 1880 as before.
It presupposed that the decline came about chiefly through a reduction in how often harvests failed.
It could not account for why grain prices in unconnected towns diverged from one another after 1880.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says historians credited hardier seeds, which ‘were thought to have made harvests less likely to fail in the first place,’ so the explanation depended on failures becoming rarer, which Maranho denies; that is D. C is the tempting trap: it was Maranho’s 1994 study, not the Brask records, that showed harvest failures did not become rarer. E distorts the data, which showed only that the gap among unconnected towns did not narrow, not that prices diverged.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer something about the old seed-variety explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P1’s last sentence, and P2’s first two sentences where Maranho rejects it.

breakdown.analysis: The old view: seeds made harvests ‘less likely to fail in the first place.’ So it worked by making failures rarer. Maranho’s point is that failures didn’t become rarer; their consequences changed. Prephrase: the old explanation depended on fewer harvest failures.

choices.note: Unsupported. The passage never says what most historians did after 1994. Possible, but you can’t pick an answer on a possibility.
Wrong explanation. Transport is the critics’ alternative to Maranho in P3. The old explanation was about seeds.

Wrong source. Maranho’s study showed that harvest failures didn’t become rarer. The Brask records are about merchants’ shipments and credit. The answer borrows a real claim and pins it on the wrong evidence.
CORRECT. Seeds were thought to make harvests ‘less likely to fail in the first place,’ so the explanation only works if failures became less frequent. That’s the presupposition Maranho attacks.
Distortion. The passage says the gap among unconnected towns ‘did not’ narrow. Not narrowing is not the same as diverging. Polar opposite vs. logical opposite.

questions.stem: The information in the passage most helps to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: Why were the agents of the Brask trading house unable to obtain credit in some valley towns?
By how much did deaths from hunger in the Torrin Valley decline between 1880 and 1900?
Before the telegraph, how did merchants in well-supplied districts usually learn of shortages in other districts?
Which towns in the Torrin Valley were the first to acquire rail links?
Did the seed varieties introduced in the 1870s raise average yields in districts lacking telegraph offices?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that before the telegraph a merchant learned of a shortage elsewhere ‘only when travelers brought the news,’ which answers C. A is tempting because the passage does say some agents could not get credit, but it never says why. The passage gives no figures for the decline in deaths (B), names no rail towns (D), and says nothing about yields by district (E).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one question the passage actually answers.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Scan for each choice’s topic: P2 for pre-telegraph news, P3 for rail links, P4 for credit.

breakdown.analysis: On ‘most helps to answer’ questions, the right answer is usually a plain detail stated in one sentence. The traps ask about something the passage mentions but doesn’t explain (why, how much, which ones). Check each choice against the text.

choices.note: Mentioned, not answered. P4 says agents in some towns ‘could not obtain credit from a local bank,’ but never says why.
No numbers. The passage says crises became ‘far less deadly’ after 1880 but gives no figures and no 1900 endpoint.
CORRECT. P2: before the telegraph, a merchant learned of a shortage elsewhere ‘only when travelers brought the news.’ Direct answer.
Not answered. P3 mentions that many connected towns got rail links in the same decade and that six towns got telegraph offices well before railways, but it never names which towns got rail first.
Not answered. The passage says seeds were thought to make failures rarer and Maranho says failures didn’t become rarer, but nothing about yields broken down by telegraph access.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen Maranho’s response to the first objection mentioned in the third paragraph?
choices: In the six towns, neither the routes by which grain was carried nor the charges for carrying it changed between the telegraph’s arrival and the railway’s.
In towns that acquired rail links before telegraph offices, the gap between their grain prices and those of other towns narrowed when the railway arrived.
Agents of grain firms in the Torrin Valley commonly ordered shipments within days of receiving telegraphed reports of rising prices.
The six towns were among the largest market towns in the Torrin Valley.
Deaths from hunger in the six towns declined further after the railways reached them.
questions.explanation: The first objection says cheaper transport, not faster news, narrowed the price gaps; Maranho replies that in six towns the gap narrowed when the telegraph arrived, years before rail. A closes the remaining loophole by ruling out some other transport improvement in those years, so the narrowing can’t be credited to cheaper carriage. C is the most tempting trap, but it addresses the second objection, about how merchants behaved, not whether transport rather than information did the work. B, if anything, supports the critics by showing rail could narrow gaps on its own.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Strengthen Maranho’s answer to the critics who credited railways (cheaper transport), not the telegraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P3: the first objection (rail links in the same decade) and her reply (six towns with telegraph seven-plus years before rail).

breakdown.analysis: Her reply: in six towns, the gap narrowed when the telegraph came, not when the railway did. Remaining hole: maybe transport got cheaper in some other way during those years (better roads, cheaper river freight) at the same time as the telegraph. A strengthener closes that hole. Prephrase: nothing else about transport changed in those towns when the telegraph arrived. It’s like proving a new coach won the games by showing the roster didn’t change.

choices.note: CORRECT. If routes and freight charges stayed the same between telegraph and railway, then cheaper transport can’t explain the narrowing that came with the telegraph. That takes out the critics’ alternative in exactly the towns Maranho relies on.
Weakens, if anything. It shows railways can narrow price gaps by themselves, which helps the critics’ claim that transport mattered. It doesn’t make her six-town evidence any stronger.

Wrong objection. Prompt shipping after telegraphed reports answers the second objection (would merchants withhold grain?). The first objection is about transport vs. information. The LSAT is ultra specific about which claim you’re supporting.
Irrelevant at best. Size doesn’t tell you whether transport or information caused the narrowing. If anything, it raises a worry that the six towns aren’t typical.
Doesn’t help. Further declines in deaths after rail arrived suggest railways mattered too. Maranho’s reply turns on what happened when the telegraph arrived, before any railway.

questions.stem: Which one of the following studies would be most useful in evaluating the claim made in the last sentence of the passage?
choices: a comparison of deaths from hunger during harvest failures in districts connected to the telegraph with those in districts that were not connected, for the decades both before and after 1880
a study of whether grain firms other than the Brask trading house also refrained from withholding stock when prices elsewhere rose

a comparison of the change in deaths during harvest failures after the telegraph arrived, between connected districts whose towns had banks lending to grain merchants and connected districts whose towns had none

a measurement of how much the gap between grain prices in towns with banks lending to grain merchants narrowed in the years after those towns acquired telegraph offices and began receiving price reports
a survey of the interest rates that banks in the Torrin Valley charged grain merchants in the decades after 1880
questions.explanation: The last sentence claims information reduced the toll of harvest failures only where merchants had the means to act on it, so the useful study compares the telegraph’s effect on deaths in places with and without merchant credit, which is C. D is the strongest trap: it looks only at towns with credit and measures prices rather than deaths, so with no comparison group it can’t show that the effect was limited to such towns. A tests whether information mattered at all, not whether its effect depended on credit.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the study that best tests the passage’s last claim.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P4’s last sentence: ‘Information... reduced the toll of harvest failures only where merchants had the means to act on it.’

breakdown.analysis: The claim has two parts: an outcome (the toll of harvest failures) and a condition (‘only where’ merchants could act, meaning had credit). To test ‘only where,’ you need a comparison: the telegraph’s effect with credit vs. without credit. A study missing the comparison group can’t test a conditional claim. Prephrase: compare the telegraph’s effect on deaths in places with lending banks and places without.

choices.note: Tests the wrong variable. Telegraph vs. no telegraph tells you whether information mattered, which is Maranho’s original thesis. It says nothing about whether credit was needed for information to matter.
Wrong question. Withholding is the second objection from P3. The last sentence is about credit, not merchants’ honesty.

CORRECT. It measures the outcome the claim is about (deaths during harvest failures), isolates the telegraph’s arrival, and compares places with merchant credit to places without. If deaths fell only where banks lent to merchants, the claim is confirmed; if they fell equally in both, it’s undercut.

Strong trap. It’s about the right factors, but it looks only at towns with credit. Without towns lacking credit to compare against, you can’t tell whether the effect was limited to credit towns. It also measures prices, not the toll in deaths.
Out of scope. Interest rates tell you about the cost of credit, not whether information helped reduce deaths only where credit was available.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: The Brask trading house had agents in each of the six towns that acquired telegraph offices before rail links.
Until the Brask records were found, the evidence that merchants did not commonly withhold grain during shortages was indirect.
The Brask records indicate that Maranho’s price data overstated how much price gaps narrowed after the telegraph arrived.
Merchants in towns where bank credit was unavailable deliberately withheld grain when prices elsewhere rose.
Once railways reached the valley’s towns, telegraphed price reports ceased to affect merchants’ shipments.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says Maranho could answer the withholding objection ‘only by appeal to the price data themselves,’ and the fourth says the Brask records first allowed merchant conduct ‘to be examined directly,’ so the earlier evidence was indirect, which is B. D is the tempting trap: the records show few shipments where agents lacked credit, which points to inability to act, not deliberate withholding. Nothing supports A’s claim that the firm operated in the six towns.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the passage best supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P3’s last sentence (Maranho’s reply to the second objection) and P4’s first sentence (the records let conduct be ‘examined directly’).

breakdown.analysis: No clear prephrase here, so test each choice against the text. Look for a choice that combines two paragraphs: P3 says Maranho’s only answer on withholding came from price data; P4 says the Brask records let conduct be examined ‘directly.’ Put together: before 2009, the evidence on withholding was indirect.

choices.note: Unsupported. The firm had agents in eleven valley towns, but the passage never says which ones or whether the six towns were among them.

CORRECT. Before the records, Maranho could answer the withholding objection ‘only by appeal to the price data,’ which is inference from prices, not observation of conduct. The records ‘allowed merchant conduct to be examined directly.’ So the earlier evidence was indirect.
Not stated. The records show prompt shipments and no withholding. Nothing says Maranho’s price data were wrong.

Distortion. Where agents lacked credit, reports ‘produced few shipments.’ That’s about not having the means to act, not a choice to hold stock back. The answer takes the passage’s own words and puts them in the wrong relationship.
Unsupported and extreme. The passage never discusses whether telegraphed reports mattered after rail arrived, and ‘ceased’ is far stronger than anything in the text.

questions.stimulus: Farmer: Agronomists warn that planting corn in the same field year after year steadily depletes the soil and lowers yields. But my neighbor Tolliver has planted corn in his east field every year for two decades, and last year his harvest there was one of the best in the county. So the agronomists' warning is greatly overstated.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the farmer's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes that a practice that does not lower yields must therefore improve the soil
fails to consider whether rotating crops would cost Tolliver more than planting corn every year
treats a single case as if it settled a claim about what generally happens
relies on a report of a neighbor's harvest that may have been exaggerated
overlooks the possibility that the agronomists' warning concerns crops other than corn
questions.explanation: The farmer rebuts a general warning about what continuous corn planting tends to do with one field that happened to do well; one exception cannot show a general tendency is overstated, which C names. D is tempting, but it only raises a possibility the argument gives no reason to suspect, and even an accurate report of one harvest would leave the flaw in place.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The agronomists' warning about planting corn year after year is greatly overstated.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Tolliver has planted corn in one field for twenty years; last year that field gave one of the county's best harvests.

breakdown.analysis: So what if one field did fine? One lucky field doesn't tell you what usually happens. Structure: 1. Experts: continuous corn tends to deplete soil and cut yields. 2. Tolliver's one field had a great year. → So the warning is overstated. This is the anecdote-versus-trend flaw (a hasty generalization from one case). It's a classic; know it. It's like: my uncle smoked and lived to 90, so the risks of smoking are exaggerated. We need an answer that says the farmer uses a single case to knock down a general claim.

choices.note: Polar vs. logical opposite. The farmer never says the practice improves soil; he only claims the harm is overstated. 'Not harmful' is not the same as 'beneficial.'
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Since this fertilizer doesn't damage the roots, it must make the plants grow faster.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The argument is about soil and yields, not about cost. Cost is never in play.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Planting corn every year is the best choice for Tolliver, since soil depletion is minor. (ignores what rotation would cost)

choices.note: CORRECT. One field doing well says almost nothing about what generally happens across many fields. This is the anecdote-versus-trend flaw.

Tempting. Doubting a neighbor's brag feels natural. But nothing suggests Tolliver exaggerated, and even a perfectly accurate report of one harvest can't overturn a general warning. You can't pick an answer on a possibility.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: My cousin says his tomato plants never got blight, so blight must be rare. (trusts a possibly biased report)

choices.note: Wrong group. The warning is explicitly about corn, and Tolliver grows corn. There's no mismatch of crops to overlook.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Experts say wheat drains the soil, but my barley field is fine, so the experts are wrong.

questions.stimulus: Editor: For forty years, the Harlow Courier has printed a weekly list of local court filings. Recently some readers have urged the paper to drop the list, calling it an invasion of privacy. The Courier should keep printing it. Court filings are public records that anyone may inspect, so printing them reveals nothing truly private. Moreover, the list is the only regular source of this information for residents who cannot get to the courthouse.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the editor's argument?
choices: The Courier should continue printing its weekly list of local court filings.
