Because court filings are public records, they are not private in any sense at all.
The Courier's list is the best available source of information about local court filings.
Readers who object to the list should have no say in the Courier's editorial decisions.
Residents who cannot get to the courthouse have no way to inspect court filings.
questions.explanation: After a background sentence and the readers' objection, the editor states the position: the Courier should keep printing the list; the public-records point and the only-source point both support it. B overstates a supporting premise ('nothing truly private' becomes 'not private in any sense'), and C turns 'only regular source' into an unsupported ranking.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Courier should keep printing the list of court filings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Filings are public records, so printing them reveals nothing truly private; the list is the only regular source for residents who can't reach the courthouse.

breakdown.analysis: Does the first sentence matter? No. 'For forty years the Courier has printed the list' is background; ignore it. Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. 1. Filings are public records → printing them reveals nothing truly private. 2. The list is the only regular source for residents who can't reach the courthouse. Both of those answer 'why keep the list?' So the conclusion is the sentence right after the objection: the Courier should keep printing it.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the editor's stated position, and both later sentences are reasons for it.

Tempting. It sounds like the editor's key point, and it's close to a premise. But it stretches 'nothing truly private' into 'not private in any sense,' and even the accurate version is support, not the conclusion.
Unsupported ranking. 'Only regular source for residents who can't get to the courthouse' is not 'best source.' The LSAT is ultra specific about words like best.
Adds a consequence the editor never mentions. Disagreeing with the objectors is not the same as saying they should have no say.
Too broad and partly opposite. The editor says the list is the only regular source for these residents, not that they have no way at all to see the filings.

questions.stimulus: Store manager: Last quarter, we offered shoppers free samples of our new house-brand granola at the store entrance. Of the shoppers who took a sample, 40 percent bought a box of the granola that same day. So the sampling stand is an effective way to boost sales of the granola.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the store manager's argument?
choices: Shoppers who took a sample were more likely than other shoppers to describe the store's prices as reasonable.
Shoppers who declined a sample tended to spend less in total during their visit than shoppers who took one.
Shoppers who are not offered samples sometimes buy food products they have never tasted.
On those same days, under 5 percent of shoppers who skipped the sample bought a box of the granola.
The granola was priced well below comparable brands sold at the store throughout the quarter.
questions.explanation: A 40 percent purchase rate among samplers means nothing without knowing the rate among shoppers who did not sample; D supplies that comparison group and shows a huge gap. E is the trap in the wrong direction: a low price is an alternative reason many shoppers bought the granola, so it weakens rather than strengthens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The sampling stand effectively boosts granola sales.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 40 percent of shoppers who took a sample bought the granola that day.

breakdown.analysis: 40 percent compared to what? If 40 percent of shoppers who never tasted it also bought a box, the stand did nothing. The manager studied only one group. This is the missing-comparison-group flaw; it's everywhere on the LSAT, so know it. It's like saying a tutor works because 80 percent of her students passed, without asking how many students passed overall. We need an answer that says shoppers who didn't sample bought the granola far less often.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Opinions about prices aren't granola sales. This doesn't show the samples made anyone buy granola.
Wrong dimension again: total spending, not granola. And it could just mean bigger spenders like free food. It says nothing about whether sampling caused granola purchases.
Wrong group and irrelevant. Shoppers who are never offered samples sometimes buying untasted foods tells you nothing about this stand.
CORRECT. This supplies the missing comparison group. 40 percent versus under 5 percent on the same days makes the stand look like it really drives sales.
Tempting, because a low price sounds like a reason sales were good. But that's the problem: it's a different reason shoppers bought the granola, competing with the sampling explanation. It weakens.

questions.stimulus: After the Eastgate branch library added Saturday story hours, it lent more children's books in a year than it ever had before. Yet that same year, for the first time in a decade, Eastgate was not the city's branch that lent the most children's books.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Most of the children who attended Eastgate's story hours already had library cards.
That year another branch doubled its children's collection, and its children's lending rose far more.
Eastgate's lending of adult fiction declined slightly in the year that story hours were added.
Saturday story hours are more popular with families of young children than weekday programs are.
Children's books lent by Eastgate are, on average, returned later than those lent by other branches.
questions.explanation: The puzzle confuses 'more than before' with 'the most of any branch'; Eastgate can set its own record while another branch grows even faster, which is exactly what B describes. C is about adult fiction, the wrong group of books, so it leaves the children's-lending puzzle untouched.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Eastgate lent more children's books than ever, but it lost its spot as the branch lending the most children's books.

breakdown.analysis: How can Eastgate lend more than ever and still lose first place? Easy: 'more than before' is a relative word; 'the most' is a ranking against every other branch. This relative-vs-absolute switch is a classic paradox engine; know it. A runner can set a personal record and still finish second. We need an answer that says another branch grew even faster.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether story-hour kids already had cards doesn't explain why another branch passed Eastgate.
CORRECT. Eastgate went up, but another branch went up more and passed it. Both facts now fit.
Wrong group. Adult fiction isn't children's books. This doesn't touch either side of the puzzle.
Tempting. Popular story hours explain why Eastgate's lending rose. But the rise is the half of the puzzle that isn't puzzling; this says nothing about why another branch passed Eastgate.
Wrong dimension. How late books come back has nothing to do with how many are lent.

questions.stimulus: Port official: In March, the Delmont Port Authority began requiring container ships to slow to 10 knots within twenty miles of the harbor. There have been no collisions between ships and the whales that feed near the harbor since then, though there were three such collisions the previous year. So the speed rule has kept whales from being struck.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the port official's argument?
choices: The speed rule is the most effective of all the measures available for protecting the whales that feed near the harbor.
More whales feed near the harbor now than did before the speed rule was adopted.
Ships obeying the speed rule have not been delayed in unloading their cargo.
Other ports where whales feed should adopt a speed rule like Delmont's.
Without the speed rule, at least one collision near the harbor would probably have occurred since March.
questions.explanation: To credit the rule with preventing collisions, the official must assume the collisions would otherwise have kept happening; negate E (without the rule there would have been no collisions anyway) and the rule saved nothing. A is the superlative trap: the rule can have prevented strikes without being the best possible measure.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The speed rule has kept whales from being struck.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Three collisions the year before the rule; zero since the rule began in March.

breakdown.analysis: So collisions stopped. Would they have stopped anyway? Maybe the whales moved, or last year's three were a fluke. Structure: 1. Rule began in March. 2. Zero collisions since; three the year before. → The rule prevented strikes. Crediting a policy for an outcome needs the outcome not to have happened anyway (the counterfactual). We need an answer that says: without the rule, collisions probably would have kept happening. Test every choice by negating it.

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds like strong support for the rule. But the rule can have prevented strikes without being the best available measure. Too strong for a required assumption.
choices.negation: The speed rule is not the most effective measure available. (The rule could still have prevented collisions, so the argument survives.)

choices.note: Not required. Take the narrowest negation: the same number of whales feed there now. That does nothing to the argument, so the argument doesn't depend on this. (More whales would only make zero collisions look more impressive.)
choices.negation: It is not the case that more whales feed near the harbor now than before. (The same number could be there; the argument still stands.)

choices.note: Wrong dimension: cost and delays, not whale safety. Negating it doesn't touch the conclusion.
choices.negation: Ships obeying the rule have been delayed in unloading cargo. (A cost, but the rule could still protect whales.)

choices.note: Adds a consequence the argument never draws. The official talks only about Delmont.
choices.negation: Other ports should not adopt a similar rule. (Irrelevant to whether Delmont's rule worked.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: even without the rule, there would have been no collisions since March. Then the rule prevented nothing, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: Even without the speed rule, there would have been no collisions near the harbor since March.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The Wexford Players' managing director claims that moving the company's season from the downtown hall to the new riverside venue will increase ticket sales, because the riverside venue has ample parking. But city surveys show that theatergoers rarely cite parking as a reason for staying home. Clearly, then, the move will not increase ticket sales.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the critic's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on surveys whose respondents may not have been representative of theatergoers in general
infers that a claim is false merely because one reason offered for it is weak
presumes that whatever does not reduce attendance must increase it
takes for granted that ticket sales are the only measure of a theater season's success
concludes that the move should not be made on the basis of evidence about parking alone
questions.explanation: The critic undercuts the director's reason (parking) and then concludes the director's claim is false, but the move could raise sales for other reasons, such as a larger hall or a more attractive location; B names this. E is tempting, but the critic never says the move should not be made, only that it won't raise sales.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The move to the riverside venue will not increase ticket sales.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The director's reason was parking; surveys say parking rarely keeps people home.

breakdown.analysis: So the parking reason is weak. Does that mean sales won't rise? No. The new venue could sell more tickets for a dozen other reasons: a nicer setting, more seats, a busier neighborhood. You might think the flaw is that the survey is shaky. But even with a perfect survey, the critic only knocks down one reason. Treating a failed argument as proof that its conclusion is false is a classic flaw; know it. It's like: 'You say this restaurant is good because it's cheap? Price doesn't matter, so the restaurant is bad.' We need an answer that says the critic infers falsehood from weak support.

choices.note: Merely possible. Nothing suggests the surveys were skewed. Even with perfect surveys, the real flaw remains.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We polled visitors at the opera house, and most prefer opera, so the city's residents prefer opera to musicals.

choices.note: CORRECT. The critic shows the parking reason is weak and then concludes the move won't raise sales. A weak reason doesn't make the claim false.
Polar vs. logical opposite, and the critic never reasons this way. Nobody here jumps from 'doesn't reduce' to 'increases.'
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new lobby won't hurt attendance, so it is sure to boost attendance.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The debate is about ticket sales only; nobody claims sales are the only measure of success.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The season sold out, so it was an artistic triumph.

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds like the critic's attitude. But the conclusion is only that sales won't rise, not that the move shouldn't happen. It adds a consequence the critic never draws.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Parking won't boost sales, so the company must not move.

questions.stimulus: Every year, codling moth larvae infest at least a few orchards in the Pell Valley. The Pell Fruit Cooperative buys apples only from orchards that it does not know to be infested. This year the cooperative bought apples from every orchard in the valley.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The cooperative does not inspect orchards for codling moth larvae before buying their apples.
Most of the apples the cooperative bought this year came from infested orchards.
Orchards known to be infested cannot sell their apples to any buyer in the valley.
This year at least one Pell Valley orchard was infested without the cooperative's knowing it.
Codling moth larvae do not reduce the quality of apples enough to concern most buyers.
questions.explanation: Some orchards were infested this year, and the cooperative bought from all of them while buying only from orchards it did not know to be infested; so at least one infested orchard was infested without the cooperative's knowledge, which is D. A is merely possible: the cooperative may inspect and simply miss infestations.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Every year, at least a few valley orchards are infested; 2) the cooperative buys only from orchards it doesn't know are infested; 3) this year it bought from every valley orchard.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to fully prephrase, but combine the facts and something drops out. 1. This year, at least a few orchards were infested. 2. Cooperative buys → it doesn't know of an infestation. 3. It bought from every orchard. Chain: infested orchard → bought from (3) → cooperative didn't know it was infested (2). So infested-but-unknown orchards exist. Watch for answers that guess at why it didn't know, or that inflate 'a few' to 'most.'

choices.note: Tempting. 'They didn't know' makes it feel like they didn't look. But the cooperative could inspect carefully and still miss larvae. We don't know this.
Too strong. 'At least a few' infested orchards says nothing about most of the apples.
Wrong group and too broad. The rule is about this one cooperative, not every buyer in the valley.
CORRECT. Infested orchards existed this year, the cooperative bought from all orchards, and it only buys when it doesn't know of an infestation. So at least one infestation went unnoticed.
Wrong dimension and unsupported. The facts say nothing about apple quality or what most buyers care about.

questions.stimulus: Climate scientist: For years, the Arvik research station measured air temperature with sensors mounted on the roof of its heated main building. In 2019 the sensors were moved to an open field 200 meters away, and the station's average recorded winter temperature since then has been 0.8°C lower than in the previous five winters. Clearly, heat escaping from the building had been inflating the earlier readings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the climate scientist's argument?
choices: At nearby stations whose sensors were never moved, average recorded winter temperatures since 2019 have also been about 0.8°C lower than in the previous five winters.
Sensors mounted on the roofs of heated buildings sometimes record temperatures higher than those of the surrounding air.
Summer temperatures recorded at the Arvik station have shown considerable variation from year to year.
The sensors installed in the open field in 2019 are a newer and more sensitive model than the ones that had previously been used on the roof.
Several other research stations in the region have also moved their sensors away from buildings in recent years.
questions.explanation: The scientist attributes the 0.8°C drop to the move, which requires that winters would not have been colder anyway; A shows the same drop at stations that never moved, so the drop is better explained by actually colder winters. D is tempting, but a newer model only weakens if we add the unstated assumption that it reads lower.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Building heat had been inflating the old rooftop readings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the sensors moved away from the building in 2019, recorded winter averages dropped 0.8°C.

breakdown.analysis: Colder readings after the move. Were winters just colder? If so, the readings would have dropped with or without the move. Structure: 1. Sensors moved from roof to field in 2019. 2. Winter averages since are 0.8°C lower. → Building heat had inflated old readings. It's a before/after causal claim that ignores an alternative cause. We need an answer that says the drop happened anyway, somewhere the sensors never moved.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same drop, no move. The likeliest explanation is that winters really were colder, so the move (and building heat) isn't needed to explain the change.
Opposite direction. This makes the scientist's explanation more plausible. It strengthens.
Wrong group (summer, not winter) and a vague word ('variation'). Year-to-year summer swings don't explain a steady winter drop.
Tempting. A new sensor model sounds like an alternative explanation. But nothing says the new model reads lower; you'd have to assume that. Merely possible.
Wrong group. Other stations moving their sensors tells you nothing about what explains Arvik's numbers.

questions.stimulus: Last year, none of the patients at Brightwater Dental whose molars were coated with sealant developed a cavity in a sealed molar. This year, every child patient at Brightwater will have sealant applied to his or her molars. So no child patient at Brightwater will develop a cavity in a sealed molar this year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Last year, every Harmon store that hired security guards reported fewer thefts. This year, no Harmon store will hire guards. So no Harmon store will report fewer thefts this year.

None of the tomato plants in Ruiz's garden developed blight this summer, and every one of them had been sprayed with a copper solution in early June. So the spray is what kept all of Ruiz's plants free of blight.
Last year, most newspapers that raised their subscription prices lost subscribers. The Ledger will raise its price this year. So the Ledger will probably lose subscribers.
None of the twenty library patrons surveyed last month had used the new self-checkout machines. So few of the library's patrons have used the machines.

Last season, no Kessler deckhand who wore the new grip gloves hurt a hand while wearing them. This season every apprentice deckhand will wear them. So no apprentice will hurt a hand while wearing them.
questions.explanation: The original takes a past pattern (no one with treatment T had outcome O), notes that a new group will all receive T, and predicts none of them will have O; E matches step for step. A is tempting because it reuses the before/after frame, but it reasons from the absence of the treatment to the absence of the outcome, a different (negated) pattern.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: No child patient will develop a cavity in a sealed molar this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year no sealed patient got a cavity in a sealed molar; this year all child patients get sealant.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Last time, no one who got T had O; now everyone in group G will get T; so no one in G will have O.

breakdown.analysis: What's the skeleton? 1. Last year, no one who got T (sealant) had O (a cavity in a sealed molar). 2. This year, everyone in group G (child patients) gets T. → No one in G will have O. Match the quantifiers: none / every / none. Kill anything that switches to 'most' or 'probably,' draws a causal conclusion about the past, generalizes from a sample, or negates the treatment. We need the answer that applies a past none-pattern to a whole new group.

choices.note: Polar flip. It says the group will NOT get the treatment and concludes it won't get the good result. That's reasoning from the absence of T, not from everyone getting T.
Different conclusion type. This draws a causal explanation about the past, not a prediction about a new group.
Tempting. Same before/after frame and a prediction for this year. But 'most' and 'probably' for a single paper aren't 'none' applied to a whole group. Close in feel, different in structure.
Different pattern entirely: a sample generalized to a population, with no treatment and no new group.
CORRECT. No glove-wearer was injured last season; every apprentice will wear the gloves; so no apprentice will be injured. Same none / every / none skeleton.

questions.stimulus:
Ines: The Ferndale Public Library should keep its reading room open until midnight during exam season. Students need a quiet place to study late that does not charge them anything, and the library is the only such place in town.

Daniel: Students do need a quiet, free place to study late. But staying open until midnight would mean paying library staff overtime from an already strained budget. The school district's study hall, which also stays open late and is free, should fill that role instead.
questions.stem: The dialogue most strongly supports the claim that Ines and Daniel agree that
choices: the library should keep its reading room open until midnight during exam season
the library is the only quiet, free place in town for students to study late
students need a quiet place to study late that costs them nothing to use
paying library staff overtime would be an unwise use of the library's budget
the school district's study hall is a better place to study than the library
questions.explanation: Ines says students need a quiet place to study late that is free, and Daniel opens by granting exactly that, so C is their shared view. B is the attractive trap: Ines asserts it, but Daniel implicitly denies it by naming the free, late-open study hall.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ines: keep the library open until midnight; students need a free, quiet late-night spot and the library is the only one.; Daniel: yes, students need that, but overtime strains the budget; the district's free study hall should do it.

breakdown.analysis: Who actually says yes to the same thing? To agree, both speakers must say yes. Daniel's first sentence is a concession: 'Students do need a quiet, free place to study late.' That echoes Ines's premise word for word. Everything else divides them: whether the library should stay open, and whether the library is the only option (Daniel names a free study hall). We need the one point both affirm.

choices.note: Opposite of agreement. Ines says yes; Daniel says the study hall should do it instead. This is what they disagree about.
Tempting. Daniel's reply starts by echoing Ines's sentence. But he then names a free study hall that stays open late, so he implicitly denies the library is the only option.
CORRECT. Ines states it as her premise; Daniel concedes it in his first sentence. Both say yes.
Ines never addresses the budget or overtime. One speaker silent means no agreement. Also the wrong dimension: cost, not need.
Unsupported ranking. Daniel says the study hall should fill the role, not that it's a better place to study. Ines says nothing about it.

questions.stimulus: Retail consultant: A store that moves to a shopping center will keep its regular customers only if those customers can easily reach the new location. All of Ostler Hardware's regular customers live downtown, and none of them owns a car. So if Ostler Hardware moves to the Brookfield shopping center, it will not keep its regular customers.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the retail consultant's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Stores that move to shopping centers usually attract enough new customers to replace those they lose.
The Brookfield shopping center cannot easily be reached by people who live downtown and do not own cars.
If a store's regular customers can easily reach its new location, the store will keep those customers.
Most of the people who shop at the Brookfield shopping center arrive there by car rather than by bus.
Ostler Hardware would lose money if it moved to the Brookfield shopping center.
questions.explanation: Keep customers → customers can easily reach the new location; so if Ostler's carless downtown customers cannot easily reach Brookfield, Ostler won't keep them, and B supplies exactly that link. D is the attractive trap: how most Brookfield shoppers arrive is about the wrong group and doesn't establish that Ostler's customers can't get there.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If Ostler moves to Brookfield, it will not keep its regular customers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Keep regulars → regulars can easily reach the new site; Ostler's regulars all live downtown and have no cars.

breakdown.analysis: So the regulars live downtown and don't drive. Who says they can't get to Brookfield? Maybe a bus runs right there. Chain: 1. Keep regulars → regulars can easily reach new site. Contrapositive: can't easily reach → won't keep. 2. Regulars: downtown, no car. Missing link: downtown + no car → can't easily reach Brookfield. Then: can't reach → won't keep. We need an answer that says Brookfield isn't easily reachable for carless downtown residents.

choices.note: Irrelevant and slightly opposite. Replacing lost customers isn't keeping regulars, and it doesn't show the regulars are lost.
CORRECT. Downtown, carless → can't easily reach Brookfield → (contrapositive of the rule) won't keep them. The conclusion follows.

Reverses the conditional. The stimulus says easy reach is necessary for keeping customers; this makes it sufficient. And it's about what happens when they CAN reach the store, which doesn't help prove they're lost.

Tempting. If most Brookfield shoppers drive, it sounds hard to reach without a car. But that's the wrong group, and a bus could still serve downtown. It doesn't guarantee the regulars can't easily get there.
Wrong dimension. Money isn't customers. The conclusion is about keeping regulars.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago, the Halcyon Line coated the hulls of its six oldest cargo ships with a new drag-reducing paint. Since then, each of these ships has burned substantially less fuel per voyage than it did before. Nevertheless, these six ships still burn more fuel per voyage than any other ship in Halcyon's fleet.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain how both of the claims above could be true?
choices: The new paint has also been applied to several ships owned by Halcyon's competitors.
Fuel prices have risen sharply in the two years since the paint was applied.
Halcyon plans to retire its six oldest ships within the next decade.
Before being painted, the six ships burned far more fuel per voyage than any other Halcyon ship did.
The paint must be reapplied every few years in order to remain effective at reducing drag on the hull.
questions.explanation: 'Burns less than before' is relative; 'burns more than any other ship' is a comparison to the rest of the fleet; if the six ships started far worse than everything else, a substantial cut can still leave them at the top, as D says. B is a wrong-dimension trap: fuel prices affect cost, not the amount of fuel burned.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The paint substantially cut each old ship's fuel use, but those ships still burn more fuel per voyage than any other Halcyon ship.

breakdown.analysis: Less fuel than before, yet still the most fuel of any ship? Sure, if they started way higher. 'Reduced' is not 'low.' Watch the switch from a relative word (less than before) to a comparison with others (more than any other ship); it's a classic paradox engine. A 300-pound person who loses 50 pounds can still be the heaviest in the office. We need an answer that says the six ships started far above the rest of the fleet.

choices.note: Wrong group. Competitors' ships don't explain the ranking within Halcyon's fleet.
So? Price changes what fuel costs, not how much fuel a ship burns. Wrong dimension.
Irrelevant future plan. Retirement doesn't explain current fuel use.
CORRECT. A big head start in fuel burn means even a substantial reduction can leave them above every other ship.
Merely possible problem. Even if the paint fades someday, the stimulus says fuel use has already dropped substantially. This doesn't explain the ranking.

questions.stimulus: Circulation manager: We surveyed everyone who canceled a subscription to the Valley Herald last year, and 70 percent of them said they had at some point complained to us about late delivery. Clearly, late delivery is what is driving subscribers away, so improving our delivery service should be our top priority.
questions.stem: The circulation manager's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: fails to consider how many of the subscribers who did not cancel had also complained about late delivery
takes for granted that subscribers who complained about late delivery did so more than once
presumes, without justification, that improving delivery service would cost less than the revenue from the subscriptions it would save
relies on the responses of former subscribers, who are likely to be hostile toward the newspaper
takes for granted that late delivery is the only problem subscribers have ever complained about
questions.explanation: The 70 percent figure only matters relative to subscribers who stayed; if 70 percent of loyal subscribers had also complained about late delivery at some point, complaints don't distinguish cancelers at all, and A identifies this missing comparison. D is the cynical-narrative trap: nothing indicates the former subscribers misreported their own complaints, which the paper could verify anyway.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Late delivery is driving subscribers away, so fixing delivery should be the top priority.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70 percent of subscribers who canceled had complained about late delivery at some point.

breakdown.analysis: 70 percent of cancelers complained. How many loyal subscribers complained? If it's also 70 percent, late delivery doesn't separate leavers from stayers at all. Structure: 1. Surveyed only cancelers. 2. 70 percent had complained about delivery. → Late delivery drives people away → fix it first. This is the missing-comparison-group flaw, a cousin of correlation-vs-causation. It's like noticing that 70 percent of people who quit a gym complained about the music, without checking current members. We need an answer that says it ignores the complaint rate among subscribers who stayed.

choices.note: CORRECT. That's the missing comparison group. Without the complaint rate among those who stayed, 70 percent tells you nothing about causes.
Irrelevant. The argument needs no assumption about repeat complaints; one complaint each is enough for the 70 percent figure.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Every reader who wrote in about typos wrote in angrily, so readers are furious about typos. (assumes each writer complained many times)

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Cost-effectiveness could matter for 'top priority,' but the core gap is causal: nothing shows late delivery causes cancellations in the first place.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Faster trucks would keep subscribers, so we should buy them. (ignores whether trucks cost more than they save)

choices.note: Tempting. 'Bitter ex-customers' is a familiar story. But nothing suggests their answers are false, and whether someone complained can be checked. Even with honest answers, the missing comparison group remains.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Former employees say the manager was unfair, but former employees are always bitter, so the manager was fair.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument doesn't need late delivery to be the only complaint, just the one driving cancellations.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Readers complained about the crossword, so the crossword must be the only thing they dislike.

questions.stimulus: Researcher: Some argue that the ice cores drilled at the Tarn Glacier last decade are too shallow to reveal anything about climate before the last ice age. That is true, but it misses the point of the project. The cores were drilled to record the past few thousand years, and they record that period in exceptional detail, since their annual layers are thick enough to be counted one by one. So the project should be judged a success.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the researcher's argument by the claim that the cores record the past few thousand years in exceptional detail?
choices: It is the main conclusion of the argument.
It is a claim that the researcher concedes but argues is irrelevant to evaluating the project.
It is offered as evidence that the cores also reveal something about climate before the last ice age.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that the cores' annual layers can be counted one by one.
It is supported by another claim in the argument and is offered as support for the argument's main conclusion.
questions.explanation: The claim about exceptional detail is supported by the countable annual layers ('since…') and in turn supports the main conclusion that the project should be judged a success, so it is an intermediate conclusion, as E says. D reverses the direction of support: the countable layers support the exceptional-detail claim, not the other way round.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Tarn Glacier project should be judged a success.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Annual layers can be counted one by one → the cores record the past few thousand years in exceptional detail → that was the project's goal → success. (The 'too shallow' objection is conceded but set aside.)

breakdown.analysis: Which claim gets support, and which claim gives it? Follow the arrows. 1. Annual layers can be counted one by one ('since…') → 2. The cores record the past few thousand years in exceptional detail → 3. That was the project's goal → the project should be judged a success. The 'too shallow' objection is conceded and set aside. A claim that receives support and also gives support is an intermediate (subsidiary) conclusion. We need an answer that says exactly that.

choices.note: No. The last sentence, 'the project should be judged a success,' is the main conclusion. The detail claim supports it.
This describes the role of a different claim: the 'too shallow' objection, which the researcher concedes but sets aside. Right passage, wrong target.
Opposite. The researcher agrees the cores reveal nothing about pre-ice-age climate.
Tempting, since it connects the two claims correctly. But it runs the arrow backward: 'since' shows the countable layers support the detail claim, not the other way around.
CORRECT. It's supported by the countable-layers claim and in turn supports the conclusion that the project succeeded.

questions.stimulus: Every adult patient of the Corwin Street dental clinic completed a survey about brushing habits. Most of the respondents claimed that they brush their teeth more thoroughly than most of the clinic's other adult patients do.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Most of the respondents who made that claim do not in fact brush more thoroughly than most of the clinic's other adult patients.
No respondent could have known whether he or she brushes more thoroughly than most of the clinic's other adult patients.
At least one respondent who made that claim does not in fact brush more thoroughly than most of the clinic's other adult patients.
Patients who brush thoroughly are less likely to need fillings than patients who do not.
Most of the clinic's adult patients brush less thoroughly than dentists recommend.
questions.explanation: Fewer than half of a group can each outdo most of the others, yet more than half of all the clinic's adult patients claimed to, so at least one claim must be false, which is C. A is the trap: if just over half made the claim and just under half are truly that thorough, only a few claims are false, not most.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Every adult patient responded; 2) most respondents (so most adult patients) claimed to brush more thoroughly than most of the other adult patients.

breakdown.analysis: How many people can beat 'most of the others'? Fewer than half. Rank everyone; you have to be in the top half. Yet more than half claimed to be there. So some claims are wrong. Worked example: 100 patients, 60 make the claim. At most 49 can truly beat more than half of the other 99. So at least 11 claims are false. But 11 of 60 isn't 'most.' Spell out the quantifier trap: some claims must be false, not most. Watch for answers that inflate 'some' to 'most' or to 'impossible to know.'

choices.note: Tempting. This is the classic quantity trap. But with 60 claimants and up to 49 true claims, only 11 are false: some, not most.
Too broad: 'impossible even in principle.' Nothing says patients can't know how they compare. Some claims are false, but others could be accurate and well founded.
CORRECT. More than half claim a spot that fewer than half can hold, so at least one claim must be false.
Adds a consequence never mentioned: fillings. The facts are only about claims and thoroughness.
Wrong standard. 'Not more thorough than most others' is about relative ranking, not about dentists' recommendations. Polar vs. logical opposite: not top half ≠ below the recommended level.

questions.stimulus: Library policy: A book should be removed from the collection if, but only if, it has not been borrowed in the past five years and either it is in poor physical condition or a newer edition of it is on the library's shelves.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the policy stated above?
choices: The Millbrook library removed a cookbook that had not been borrowed in seven years and whose binding had fallen apart, even though no newer edition was available.
The Millbrook library removed a travel guide in good condition that had not been borrowed in six years, because a newer edition of it had been ordered.
The Millbrook library kept an atlas in poor condition that had not been borrowed in eight years, because a patron had recently asked about it.
The Millbrook library removed a novel in poor condition that had last been borrowed three years ago, since a newer edition was on its shelves.
The Millbrook library removed a biography in excellent condition that had not been borrowed in ten years, because it was the library's least-borrowed biography.
questions.explanation: Removal requires both no borrowing in five years and (poor condition or a newer edition on the shelves); the cookbook meets the five-year test and is in poor condition, so A conforms. B is the near-miss trap: a newer edition that has only been ordered is not on the library's shelves, so the travel guide fails the second requirement.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Remove ⟺ (not borrowed in 5 years) AND (poor condition OR newer edition on the shelves). If both parts hold, remove; if either part fails, keep.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The library's judgment must match the policy: a removed book must be (1) unborrowed for 5+ years AND (2) in poor condition OR have a newer edition on the shelves; a kept book must fail one of those parts.

breakdown.analysis: Does each book pass every test? The policy is a two-part gate. 1. Not borrowed in the past 5 years (required). 2. Poor condition OR a newer edition on the shelves (one of these). Both parts → remove. Either part fails → keep. Each trap satisfies only part: a newer edition merely on order, a borrowing three years ago, a book kept when both parts are met, or a ranking ('least-borrowed') the policy never mentions.

choices.note: CORRECT. Seven years unborrowed (part 1) and a broken binding (poor condition satisfies part 2). Removal is required, and the library removed it. No newer edition is needed since the 'or' is already met.

Tempting. Six years unborrowed, and a newer edition exists. But the edition is only on order, so it isn't 'on the library's shelves,' and the book is in good condition. The 'or' condition is left unmet.
Violates the policy. Both parts are met (eight years, poor condition), so the atlas should go. A patron's question isn't a condition the policy recognizes.
Fails part 1. Borrowed three years ago means it has been borrowed in the past five years, so it must stay.
Fails part 2: excellent condition and no newer edition mentioned. 'Least-borrowed' is a ranking the policy never uses.

questions.stimulus: Agricultural extension agent: Dairy farms in Quill County that switched their herds to locally grown alfalfa last year saw average milk output per cow rise by 8 percent, while farms that kept their old feed saw no change. Therefore, Quill County dairy farms that switch to locally grown alfalfa can expect their cows' milk output to rise.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the agent's argument?
choices: Locally grown alfalfa costs more per ton than the feed that most Quill County dairy farms now use.
Most of the farms that switched to alfalfa last year also installed newer milking equipment that same year.
Milk output per cow can be affected by the breed of the cows in a herd.
Some dairy farms in neighboring counties have also switched to locally grown alfalfa.
Cows fed locally grown alfalfa produce milk with a slightly higher fat content than cows fed other feeds.
questions.explanation: The agent attributes the 8 percent rise to the feed, but B shows that the switching farms also upgraded their milking equipment, a rival explanation for the rise. C is tempting but vague: breed 'can affect' output, yet nothing says the two groups of farms differed in breed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Farms that switch to local alfalfa can expect milk output to rise.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Farms that switched last year rose 8 percent; farms that didn't switch saw no change.

breakdown.analysis: So the switching farms improved. Was it the feed? What else changed at those farms? Structure: 1. Switchers' output rose 8 percent. 2. Non-switchers: no change. → Switching to alfalfa raises output. This is correlation treated as causation: the groups might differ in something else. We need an answer that says the switching farms also changed something else that boosts milk.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Cost isn't milk output. The agent only claims output will rise, not that switching pays off.
CORRECT. A second change at the same farms in the same year could explain the rise. The feed may have done nothing.
Tempting. Breed really can affect output. But nothing says the switchers and non-switchers had different breeds, so it doesn't explain the gap. Vague word stretched.
Wrong group. Neighboring counties' farms switching tells you nothing about why Quill's switchers improved.
Wrong dimension (fat content, not quantity), and if anything it's a small point in the feed's favor.

questions.stimulus: Retail analyst: To save on wages, Pellam's Home Supply plans to staff fewer checkout lanes on weekday mornings, when few customers shop. But many of its weekday-morning customers are contractors buying supplies in bulk before work, the store's biggest spenders. So the plan risks costing Pellam's more in lost sales than it saves in wages.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the retail analyst's argument depends?
choices: Contractors account for most of Pellam's total sales.
Weekday-morning wages make up the largest share of Pellam's labor costs.
Customers who shop on weekend afternoons are less bothered by long checkout lines than contractors shopping on weekday mornings are.
Pellam's managers have not considered reducing staffing at other times of the week.
Longer waits at checkout on weekday mornings would lead at least some contractors to buy less at Pellam's.
questions.explanation: The predicted lost sales only happen if the reduced staffing actually drives some contractors to spend less; negate E (no contractor would buy less despite longer waits) and the risk disappears. A is the too-strong trap: the contractors can be the store's biggest spenders, and losing their business can be costly, without their making up most of total sales.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The staffing cut risks losing more in sales than it saves in wages.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many weekday-morning shoppers are contractors, the biggest spenders.

breakdown.analysis: Big spenders shop on weekday mornings. So what? Do they actually buy less if the lines get longer? If they wait patiently and buy the same, nothing is lost. Structure: 1. Fewer lanes on weekday mornings. 2. Many of those shoppers are contractors, the biggest spenders. → Risk of losing more in sales than saved in wages. Missing link: the longer waits cause some contractors to spend less. Necessary assumptions are usually modest ('at least some'). Negate each choice and see which one breaks the argument.

choices.note: Tempting. If contractors are the biggest spenders, they sound like most of the business. But being the biggest spenders doesn't mean making up most of total sales, and the argument works either way. Too strong.
choices.negation: Contractors do not account for most of Pellam's total sales. (Losing some of them could still cost more than the wage savings; argument survives.)

choices.note: Unsupported ranking. The argument compares lost sales with the wage savings, wherever those wages rank.
choices.negation: Weekday-morning wages are not the largest share of labor costs. (Doesn't touch the argument.)

choices.note: Wrong group. Weekend shoppers are irrelevant to a weekday-morning plan.
choices.negation: Weekend-afternoon shoppers are not less bothered by lines than contractors. (No effect.)

choices.note: Irrelevant. What managers have or haven't considered elsewhere doesn't affect this plan's risk.
choices.negation: Pellam's managers have considered reducing staffing at other times. (No effect.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: no contractor would buy any less, however long the wait. Then there are no lost sales, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: Longer weekday-morning checkout waits would not lead any contractors to buy less at Pellam's.

questions.stimulus: Dramaturg: Some critics define a 'repertory company' as any theater company that stages several different plays in a single season. But consider a company that stages five plays in a season, hiring a separate cast for each production and never reusing an actor. No one would call that a repertory company, since the hallmark of repertory is a stable group of actors who perform together across productions.
questions.stem: The dramaturg's argument proceeds by
choices: describing a case that clearly counts as a repertory company but that the critics' definition fails to include
arguing that the critics' definition should be rejected because few theater companies actually satisfy it
showing that the critics' definition implies that every theater company is a repertory company
describing a case that satisfies the critics' definition but that clearly does not count as a repertory company
suggesting that the critics proposed their definition in order to praise companies they already favored
questions.explanation: The five-play company with a new cast each time meets the critics' definition (several plays in one season) yet is plainly not a repertory company, so the dramaturg shows the definition is too broad, as D says. A is the mirror-image trap: it describes showing a definition is too narrow (it leaves out a real case), which is the opposite move.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Implied) The critics' definition of a repertory company is wrong: it's too broad.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A company staging five plays with a fresh cast for each meets the definition but isn't repertory, since repertory requires a stable ensemble.

breakdown.analysis: Does the hypothetical company fit the critics' definition? Yes, five plays in one season. Is it a repertory company? The dramaturg says no. Fits the definition but isn't the real thing → the definition is too broad. The opposite move (a real case the definition leaves out) shows a definition is too narrow. Know both; the LSAT loves to swap them. Like defining 'bird' as 'any animal that flies' and pointing to a bat. We need an answer that says: a case satisfies the definition but clearly isn't a repertory company.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the other standard way to attack a definition. But it's the 'too narrow' attack. The dramaturg's company isn't a repertory company and it isn't excluded by the definition. Both halves are backwards.
choices.example: Example of this method: Defining a newspaper as 'a daily printed paper' is wrong, since a weekly town paper is clearly a newspaper yet isn't daily.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. How many companies meet the definition is never discussed; the attack is on accuracy, not popularity.
choices.example: Example of this method: That definition of 'great actor' is useless, since hardly anyone meets it.

choices.note: Too broad a claim. One counterexample shows the definition lets in a wrong case, not that it lets in every company. Companies staging a single play wouldn't meet it.
choices.example: Example of this method: If 'athlete' means anyone who moves, then every living person is an athlete.

choices.note: CORRECT. The company meets the critics' definition (several plays, one season) but clearly isn't repertory. That shows the definition is too broad.
Social-autopilot. Nothing about the critics' motives appears; the dramaturg argues purely from a case.
choices.example: Example of this method: The critics only define 'repertory' that way because their favorite theater happens to fit it.

questions.stimulus: Logistics analyst: Shipping firms that route cargo through the Varn Strait rather than around the Kell Peninsula save four days per voyage. Yet many firms still avoid the strait. The most likely reason is that insurers charge far higher premiums for voyages through the strait, enough to wipe out the savings from the shorter route.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the logistics analyst's argument?
choices: The Varn Strait is narrower than most of the other shipping lanes in the region.
Pirate attacks on cargo ships passing through the Varn Strait have become steadily more frequent over the course of the past decade.
Until insurers introduced higher premiums for strait voyages six years ago, most shipping firms routed their cargo through the strait.
Most firms that use the Varn Strait are larger than the firms that avoid it.
Insurers charge higher premiums for voyages around the Kell Peninsula during the winter storm season.
questions.explanation: If premiums are what keeps firms out, firms should have started avoiding the strait when the premiums appeared; C shows the timing matches that mechanism, since most firms used the strait until the higher premiums arrived. B is tempting because piracy might also raise premiums, but as stated it offers a rival reason for avoiding the strait (danger to ships and crews), so it weakens rather than strengthens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Firms avoid the Varn Strait mainly because insurance premiums for it are high enough to cancel the time savings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The strait saves four days, yet many firms avoid it.

breakdown.analysis: Premiums are the 'most likely reason'? Why not danger, narrow channels, or something else? Structure: 1. The strait saves four days. 2. Many firms avoid it anyway. → Because insurers charge premiums that wipe out the savings. A good way to strengthen a causal claim is timing that matches the mechanism: if premiums cause the avoidance, avoidance should start when the premiums started. We need an answer that ties the avoidance to the premiums, not to some other drawback.

choices.note: Merely possible. A narrow strait might be harder to navigate, which is a competing reason to avoid it, if anything. It doesn't tie avoidance to premiums.

Tempting. Piracy might push premiums up, which sounds like support. But as stated it's a separate reason to avoid the strait (danger to ships and crews). You'd have to assume it works only through premiums. It weakens.
CORRECT. The avoidance started when the premiums did. Timing that matches the proposed mechanism is solid support for the causal claim.
Vague and irrelevant. Firm size doesn't say anything about why the smaller firms avoid the strait; it's a different possible explanation, not support for premiums.
Wrong group (the other route) and opposite direction. Higher premiums around the peninsula would make the strait relatively more attractive, deepening the puzzle.

questions.stimulus: Funding officer: The Climate Data Trust funds a research proposal only if the proposal guarantees that its data will be made public within a year of collection. No proposal that relies on data licensed from a private weather firm can make that guarantee, since such firms restrict publication. Dr. Okafor's proposal on coastal fog relies on data from the Merrin Observatory. So the Trust will not fund Dr. Okafor's proposal.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the funding officer's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If a proposal guarantees that its data will be made public within a year, the Trust will fund it.
Unless data is licensed from a private weather firm, it is not data from the Merrin Observatory.
Most of the data from the Merrin Observatory is licensed from private weather firms.
Dr. Okafor's proposal does not rely on any data that is already publicly available.
Private weather firms restrict publication of all of the data they collect, whether licensed or not.
questions.explanation: Funded → guarantee; relies on privately licensed data → no guarantee; so the officer needs Okafor's Merrin data to be privately licensed data, and B, phrased as a contrapositive, says that all Merrin data is licensed from a private weather firm. C is the near miss: if only most Merrin data is licensed, Okafor's proposal might rely solely on the unlicensed remainder.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Trust will not fund Okafor's proposal.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Funded → guarantees publication within a year; relies on private-firm licensed data → can't guarantee; Okafor relies on Merrin Observatory data.

breakdown.analysis: Okafor uses Merrin data. Who says that's private, licensed data? Chain: 1. Funded → guarantees publication within a year. 2. Relies on private-firm licensed data → can't guarantee. So: licensed private data → no guarantee → not funded. 3. Okafor relies on Merrin data. Missing link: Merrin data → licensed from a private firm. Choice B says 'Unless licensed from a private firm, not Merrin data.' Unless X, not Y means Y → X: Merrin → licensed private. That's the link, written in contrapositive form. Awkward, but airtight.

choices.note: Reverses the conditional. The guarantee is necessary for funding, not sufficient. And this is about who gets funded, which can't prove Okafor won't be.
CORRECT. Translate: Merrin data → licensed from a private firm. Then Okafor relies on licensed private data → no guarantee → no funding.
Tempting. 'Most' Merrin data being licensed sounds nearly enough. But Okafor might use only the unlicensed part. A sufficient assumption has to guarantee the link, and 'most' leaves a gap.
Wrong group of data. Whether Okafor uses other public data doesn't tell us whether the Merrin data is privately licensed.
Too broad and still missing the link. Even if private firms restrict everything, nothing says Merrin is (or licenses from) a private firm.

questions.stimulus: Dentist: A crown fitted by Dr. Lin will last at least ten years if the patient avoids chewing ice. Ms. Ortiz's crown was fitted by Dr. Lin, but Ms. Ortiz chews ice regularly. So her crown will not last ten years.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the dentist's argument?
choices: A container shipped by Norrland Freight will arrive within a week if it clears customs on its first inspection. One Norrland container did not arrive within a week. So it did not clear customs on its first inspection.
If a newspaper's investigative series wins a regional award, the paper's circulation rises. The Gazette's circulation rose this year. So its investigative series must have won a regional award.
A library card will be renewed automatically if the patron has no overdue fines. Mr. Hale is a patron with no overdue fines. So his library card will be renewed automatically.
The new mouthwash has been shown not to harm tooth enamel. Anything that does not harm tooth enamel is safe to use daily. So the mouthwash is good for tooth enamel.

Every apprentice in the Tallis company who completes the stage-combat course is cleared to perform fight scenes. Joaquin is a Tallis apprentice, but he has not completed the course. Hence he is not cleared to perform fight scenes.
questions.explanation: The dentist treats avoiding ice as necessary for a Lin crown to last, when it was only stated as sufficient (Lin crown and no ice → lasts; Ortiz chews ice; so it won't last), and E denies the condition in the same way. A is the trap: it mirrors the dentist's wording almost exactly but reasons by the valid contrapositive (no fast arrival → didn't clear customs), so it is not flawed at all; B is flawed but in a different way (it affirms the result).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ms. Ortiz's crown will not last ten years.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lin crown AND avoids ice → lasts 10+ years; Ortiz has a Lin crown but chews ice.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Members of group G with condition C get result R; this member of G lacks C; so this member won't get R. (Denying the sufficient condition.)

breakdown.analysis: Ortiz chews ice. Does that doom her crown? No: avoiding ice was given as enough for the crown to last, not as required. Chain: Lin crown AND avoids ice → lasts 10+ years. Ortiz: Lin crown, chews ice. → Won't last. That's denying the sufficient condition (mistaking a sufficient condition for a necessary one), a classic; know it. Valid moves: avoids ice → lasts (forward), or didn't last → didn't avoid ice (contrapositive). The trap copies the wording but runs the contrapositive, which is valid. We need an answer that commits the same mistake, whatever the wording.

choices.note: Tempting. Same sentence shape as the dentist's: 'will ... if ...', then a fact, then a 'not' conclusion. But it's the contrapositive: didn't arrive → didn't clear customs. That's valid. A valid argument can't match a flawed one.
Flawed, but a different flaw. This reverses the conditional: circulation rose → award, affirming the result instead of denying the condition. Not the same mistake.
Valid. No fines → renewed; Hale has no fines; so renewed. Straight forward application, no flaw.
A different flaw: it treats 'does not harm' as 'is good for' (polar vs. logical opposite). No conditional is being negated.

CORRECT. Tallis apprentice who completes the course → cleared. Joaquin hasn't completed it, so 'not cleared.' Same mistake: the course is sufficient, not shown to be necessary. Different wording ('every... who'), same skeleton.

questions.stimulus: Media critic: Many people assume that local newspapers are closing because readers now prefer to get their news online. But each of the Fallowmere newspapers that closed this decade had a growing readership, in print and online combined, right up until the year it shut down. What those papers lost was their revenue from classified ads, which moved to free websites. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the media critic's argument?
choices: the closures of Fallowmere's newspapers are better explained by a loss of revenue than by a loss of readers
Fallowmere's newspapers closed because their readers came to prefer getting their news online
a local newspaper can survive only if it stops relying on classified advertising for revenue
news from online sources is less reliable than news reported by local newspapers
no newspaper anywhere has ever closed because of a decline in the number of people who read it
questions.explanation: The critic pushes back on the popular reader-flight explanation by showing readership kept growing while classified revenue vanished, so the natural completion is that revenue loss, not reader loss, explains the closures: A. B is the trap: it repeats the very popular view the critic is arguing against.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Popular view: papers close because readers moved online; 2) the closed Fallowmere papers had growing combined readership until they closed; 3) they lost classified-ad revenue to free websites.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase word for word, but the direction is clear. 1. Popular view: papers close because readers moved online. 2. The closed Fallowmere papers had growing readership until they closed. 3. They lost classified-ad revenue to free websites. The critic is pushing back on the popular view, so the blank should land where the evidence points: readers didn't leave; money did. When an author pushes back on a popular view, the trap usually repeats the popular view. We need an answer that says revenue loss, not reader loss, explains the closures.

choices.note: CORRECT. Readership grew while ad revenue vanished, so revenue loss explains the closures better than reader loss. Modest and well supported.
Tempting, because it's the familiar story. But it repeats the popular view the critic is rejecting; the critic's evidence is that readership kept growing. Social autopilot.
Too strong and adds a consequence. Losing classified revenue hurt these papers, but that doesn't make dropping classifieds the only path to survival.
Wrong dimension. The argument is about why papers closed, not about the quality of online news.
Way too broad. Evidence about Fallowmere this decade can't support a claim about every newspaper ever.

questions.stimulus: Theater board member: The Calder Players' staging of Ashfall should win this year's regional award for best production. Under the award's rules, the prize must go to the season's finest production, and Ashfall was the finest production of the season, since no other production staged this season equaled it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the board member's reasoning?
choices: It relies on the judgment of someone who has a personal stake in the outcome.
It takes for granted that the award's rules are fair to every eligible production.
It presumes that a production that was not the season's worst must have been its best.
It offers, as support for a claim, a statement that merely restates that claim.
It fails to consider that the critics might disagree about which production was finest.
questions.explanation: The only support for 'Ashfall was the finest production' is that no other production equaled it, which is the same claim in different words, so the argument assumes what it needs to prove: D. A is the tempting cynical answer, but the board member's position doesn't make the reasoning bad, and attacking the speaker would itself be a flaw; nothing in the argument appeals to the member's own authority.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ashfall should win the best-production award.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The award must go to the season's finest production; Ashfall was the finest, since no other production equaled it.

breakdown.analysis: Why was Ashfall the finest? Because no other production equaled it. Isn't that just 'it was the finest' again? Yes. Structure: 1. The award must go to the season's finest production. 2. Ashfall was the finest, since no other production equaled it. → Ashfall should win. Premise 1 is fine; the support for premise 2 restates it. That's circular reasoning (begging the question). It's a classic; know it. Circular reasoning is rarely the right answer, but here the premise really is the conclusion in disguise. Like: 'This is the best pizza in town, because no pizza in town is as good.'

choices.note: Tempting. A board member may well be biased. But bias doesn't make the reasoning flawed, and the argument never rests on the speaker's authority. Judge the argument, not the arguer.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The coach says our team is the best, and coaches know their sport, so our team is the best.

choices.note: Wrong dimension: is vs. should. The argument applies the rules as written; whether they're fair is beside the point.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The rule gives the prize to the top seller, so the prize is fairly awarded.

choices.note: Polar vs. logical opposite, but the board member never reasons from 'not the worst.' Nothing like that appears.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our show wasn't the season's worst, so it must have been the best.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'No other production equaled it' just restates 'it was the finest.' The key claim gets no independent support.
Merely possible, and irrelevant to the logic. Critics disagreeing wouldn't show Ashfall wasn't finest; the real problem is that the argument gives no evidence that it was.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The award must go to Ashfall, since everyone agrees it was the best (ignores possible dissent).

questions.stimulus: Store owner: Our clothing store has always given full refunds on unworn returns. Lately a few customers have bought expensive dresses, worn them once to an event, and returned them. Some staff want us to stop accepting dress returns altogether. But that would penalize the many honest customers who return dresses that don't fit. Instead, we should accept a dress return only if the original hang tag, which must be cut off before the dress can be worn, is still attached.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the store owner's reasoning?
choices: A store should never change a long-standing policy merely because a few of its customers have found ways to abuse it.
Honest customers should never be made to bear any of the costs created by the actions of dishonest customers.
When some customers abuse a policy, a store should stop the abuse in a way that keeps the policy's benefits for honest users.
A store's return policy should be designed above all to maximize the store's profits, even at some cost to customer goodwill.
Customers who are found to have returned worn merchandise should be barred from making further purchases.
questions.explanation: The owner rejects a blanket ban because it would hurt honest returners and endorses a tag rule that blocks the wear-once abuse while still letting honest customers return ill-fitting dresses; C endorses exactly that kind of targeted response. B is the strongest trap: it supports rejecting the ban but says nothing in favor of adopting the tag requirement (which itself places a small new condition on honest customers), and A would forbid the owner's own policy change.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Rather than banning dress returns, the store should accept them only with the hang tag still attached.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A few customers wear dresses once and return them; a ban would penalize honest customers returning dresses that don't fit; the tag must be cut off to wear the dress.

breakdown.analysis: Why is the tag rule better than a ban? Because it blocks the wear-once trick and still lets honest customers return dresses that don't fit. The owner makes two moves: 1. Reject the blanket ban (it hurts honest returners). 2. Adopt the tag rule (wearers must cut the tag; honest returners don't). A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, so it must support both moves. We need an answer that says: answer abuse with a fix that stops it without taking the benefit away from proper users.

choices.note: Too strong, and it backfires: the owner IS changing the policy (adding the tag requirement) because of a few abusers. This principle would condemn the owner's own recommendation.

Tempting. It supports rejecting the ban. But it doesn't tell you to adopt the tag rule, and the new tag condition itself puts a small burden on honest customers. Only half the conclusion is justified.

CORRECT. It calls for a response that stops the abuse (wearers can't keep the tag) while keeping the benefit for proper users (ill-fitting dresses still come back). That covers both halves of the owner's reasoning.
Wrong dimension. The owner reasons about fairness to honest customers, not profit. A profit-first principle might even favor the ban.
Adds a consequence the owner never proposes. Banning abusers isn't part of the plan and doesn't justify the tag rule.
